lessons.title: How much activity do we need? (WHO guidelines)

scenes.text: The Iyer family in Chennai — dad Ganesh (45, desk job), mum Lata (42), Meenu (14) and grandma Kamala (70) — realise none of them moves much.
Meenu finds the WHO activity guidelines for a school project and makes a chart for each person.
They start evening walks, Meenu joins the school football club, grandma does balance exercises with a chair.
Three months later, everyone sleeps better and grandma says climbing stairs feels easier.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body:
This is general education, not medical advice. **Consult a doctor before starting if you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, diabetes, asthma, a joint or back problem, are pregnant, or are recovering from an injury or illness.**

Stop at once and seek help if you feel chest pain, faintness, unusual breathlessness, or sharp pain. In an emergency in India call **112**.

steps.title: Children and teens (5–17 years)
steps.body:
WHO (2020) recommends:

- An **average of at least 60 minutes a day** of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, mostly aerobic (running, cycling, sports, active play).
- **Vigorous** activities and activities that **strengthen muscle and bone** on at least **3 days a week**.
- **Limit sedentary time**, especially recreational screen time.

steps.title: Adults (18–64 years)
steps.body:
- At least **150–300 minutes a week of moderate** aerobic activity (e.g., brisk walking), **or 75–150 minutes of vigorous** activity (e.g., running), or a mix.
- **Muscle-strengthening** activities involving all major muscle groups on **2 or more days a week**.
- Reduce sitting; **some activity is better than none** — and more brings extra benefits.

steps.title: Older adults (65+) and the very young
steps.body:
- **65+**: the adult recommendations **plus** varied activities that emphasise **balance and strength** on **3 or more days a week**, to improve function and prevent falls.
- **Under-5s** (WHO 2019): lots of active play through the day — for 3–4-year-olds at least 180 minutes of varied activity, including at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous; babies should have floor-based play and tummy time.

steps.title: Worked example: hitting 150 minutes
steps.body: Ganesh walks briskly 30 minutes on 5 weekdays = **150 minutes** of moderate activity. He adds 2 short strength sessions (20 minutes each) at home. Target met. Lata prefers jogging: 3 × 25 minutes = **75 minutes** of vigorous activity — also meets the guideline.

steps.title: What counts as moderate or vigorous?
steps.body:
- **Moderate**: you breathe faster and feel warmer but **can still talk** (not sing) — brisk walking, easy cycling, dancing, gardening.
- **Vigorous**: you **can only say a few words** before needing a breath — running, fast cycling, competitive sports, skipping.

Try this: tomorrow, use the talk test during your walk and see whether it's moderate.

activity.label: Your weekly minutes of moderate activity (adult)

bands.text: No activity yet. Start small: a 10-minute walk after meals counts.
Some activity — great start! Every extra 10 minutes helps. Build towards 150.
You meet the WHO guideline (150–300 min). Add strength 2×/week.
Above 300 minutes — additional benefits. Make sure you recover and sleep well.

quiz.q: How much activity does WHO recommend for 5–17-year-olds?
options: An average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity
quiz.why: At least 60 minutes a day on average.

quiz.q: Adults should do muscle-strengthening on at least…
quiz.why: 2 or more days a week.

quiz.q: 75 minutes of vigorous activity is roughly equivalent to…
quiz.why: Vigorous counts about double.

quiz.q: What extra do older adults need?
options: Balance and strength activities 3+ days a week
quiz.why: Multicomponent activity helps prevent falls.

quiz.q: In the talk test, moderate activity means…
options: You can talk but not sing
quiz.why: That's the classic moderate-intensity cue.

sources: WHO Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (2020)

lessons.title: Warm-up and cool-down done right

scenes.text: Rahul, 28, a software engineer in Gurugram, rushes from office to weekend football with no warm-up.
Ten minutes in, he sprints and feels a sharp pain at the back of his thigh. Three weeks out.
His physio, Dr. Mehta, gives him a 10-minute warm-up routine.
He hasn't been injured since — and he plays better in the first ten minutes.

steps.title: Why warm up?
steps.body: A good warm-up **raises body and muscle temperature**, increases heart rate and blood flow, improves joint range of motion and 'switches on' the nervous system. It prepares you physically and mentally, and structured warm-ups (like FIFA 11+ in football) have been shown to reduce injuries.

steps.title: The RAMP framework
steps.body:
- **R — Raise**: 3–5 minutes of easy movement to raise heart rate and temperature (jog, skipping, cycling).
- **A — Activate**: wake up key muscles — glute bridges, band walks, planks.
- **M — Mobilise**: dynamic movements through range — leg swings, walking lunges with a twist, arm circles, inchworms.
- **P — Potentiate**: gradually build to the intensity of your session — strides, jumps, sport-specific drills.

Total: about **8–15 minutes**.

steps.title: Static stretching: before or after?
steps.body: Long static stretches (holding a stretch for a minute or more) right before explosive activity can slightly reduce power and speed for a short time. So before sport, prefer **dynamic** movements. Short static holds are fine if followed by dynamic work. Save longer **static stretching** for the **cool-down** or a separate flexibility session.

steps.title: The cool-down
steps.body:
- 3–5 minutes of easy movement (walk, slow jog) to bring heart rate down gradually.
- Gentle **static stretches** for the muscles you used: 20–30 seconds each, no bouncing, no pain.
- Rehydrate and refuel.

A cool-down won't prevent next-day soreness completely, but it helps you relax and recover, and is a good time to improve flexibility.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping the warm-up 'to save time'.
- Going straight into sprints or heavy lifts.
- Bouncing in stretches (ballistic stretching) without training.
- Stretching into pain — mild tension is enough.

activity.prompt: Order the RAMP warm-up correctly.
items: Raise: easy jog or skipping for 3–5 minutes

quiz.why: Raise heart rate and temperature.

quiz.q: Before explosive sport, which stretching is preferred?
quiz.why: Dynamic warm-ups prepare without reducing power.

quiz.q: How long might a typical warm-up take?
quiz.why: About 8–15 minutes.

quiz.q: A cool-down mainly helps you…
options: Bring heart rate down gradually and relax; good time for static stretching
quiz.why: It eases the transition to rest.

lessons.title: Cardio: heart rate, intensity and building endurance

scenes.text: Fatima, 35, a teacher in Lucknow, signs up for a 5 km charity run but has never run before.
She starts with walk–run intervals: 1 minute jog, 2 minutes walk.
Every week she runs a little more. She uses the talk test to stay comfortable.
Eight weeks later she runs the whole 5 km, smiling.

steps.title: What cardio does
steps.body: Aerobic ('cardio') exercise uses large muscle groups rhythmically for a sustained time: walking, running, cycling, swimming, dancing, skipping. Regular cardio strengthens the heart and lungs, helps control blood pressure, blood sugar and weight, improves mood and sleep, and lowers the risk of many chronic diseases.

steps.title: Measuring intensity
steps.body:
- **Talk test**: moderate = can talk, not sing; vigorous = only a few words.
- **RPE (rating of perceived exertion)** on 0–10: about **3–4** moderate, **5–6** hard, **7–8** very hard.
- **Heart rate**: a rough estimate of maximum heart rate is **220 − age** (individuals can differ by 10 beats or more). Moderate is roughly 64–76% of max; vigorous about 77–95%.

Some medicines (e.g., beta-blockers) lower heart rate — use RPE/talk test instead.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Fatima is 35. Estimated max HR = 220 − 35 = **185 bpm**. Moderate zone ≈ 0.64 × 185 to 0.76 × 185 ≈ **118 to 141 bpm**. She checks her pulse or watch: 130 bpm while jogging — moderate. Remember it's an estimate.

steps.title: Building endurance: walk–run plan
steps.body:
- Week 1–2: 6 × (1 min jog + 2 min walk), 3 times a week.
- Week 3–4: 5 × (2 min jog + 1 min walk).
- Week 5–6: 3 × (5 min jog + 1 min walk).
- Week 7–8: 20–30 min continuous easy jog.

Repeat a week if it felt too hard. Consistency beats intensity.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Consult a doctor before starting if you have heart, lung, blood pressure, diabetes or joint conditions, or are pregnant. Stop immediately for chest pain, pain spreading to arm/jaw, fainting or severe breathlessness — call **112**. In heat, go early morning or evening and hydrate.

quiz.q: A walk–run plan works mainly because…
quiz.why: Gradual progression and consistency.

lessons.title: HIIT: high-intensity interval training, safely

story.title: Twenty minutes in a hostel room

scenes.text: Aman, 20, an engineering student in a small hostel room in Kota, has no gym and little time.
He learns a bodyweight HIIT session: 30 seconds hard, 30 seconds easy.
At first he goes all-out with sloppy form and his knees ache.
He slows down, fixes his form, and does it 2–3 times a week. He feels fitter in a month.

steps.title: What HIIT is
steps.body:
**High-intensity interval training** alternates short bursts of hard effort (for example RPE 7–9) with easy recovery. Sessions are short (10–25 minutes plus warm-up) and can improve aerobic fitness efficiently.

Examples:
- **30:30** — 30 s hard, 30 s easy, × 8–10.
- **40:20** — 40 s hard, 20 s rest.
- **Tabata-style** — 20 s very hard, 10 s rest, × 8 (4 minutes); very demanding — not for beginners.

steps.title: A beginner bodyweight HIIT
steps.body:
Warm-up 5 minutes (march, arm circles, squats). Then 2 rounds of:

- 30 s **brisk marching or jogging on the spot** / 30 s rest
- 30 s **squats** / 30 s rest
- 30 s **incline push-ups** (hands on a bed or wall) / 30 s rest
- 30 s **step-ups** on a low, stable step / 30 s rest
- 30 s **mountain climbers (slow)** / 30 s rest

Cool down 5 minutes. Do 2–3 times a week, not on consecutive days.

steps.title: Who should be careful
steps.body:
Consult a doctor before HIIT if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, are pregnant, are older and unaccustomed to exercise, or have joint problems. Beginners should first build a base of moderate activity for a few weeks.

**Form beats speed**: when form breaks down, slow down or stop. Low-impact options (marching instead of jumping, step-ups instead of jump squats) protect joints.

steps.title: Common HIIT mistakes
steps.body:
- Doing HIIT every day — you need recovery.
- Choosing complex jumping moves too soon.
- No warm-up.
- Thinking 'more sweat = better'. Quality matters more.

lessons.title: Principles: overload, reps, sets, rest and breathing

scenes.text: Divya, 24, from Jaipur, follows a different online workout every day and never seems to get stronger.
Her trainer, Mr. Thomas, asks: 'What did you lift last week?' She has no idea.
They start a simple log: same exercises, small increases each week.
In 12 weeks her squat goes from bodyweight to holding a 16 kg weight with good form.

steps.title: Before you lift
steps.body: This is general education, not medical advice. **Consult a doctor before starting if you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, diabetes, a joint or back problem, are pregnant, or are recovering from an injury.** Learn form with light loads, ideally with a qualified coach. Sharp pain = stop.

steps.title: Progressive overload
steps.body:
Muscles and bones adapt when challenged a little more than they're used to, then given time to recover. Progress by **one** small change at a time:

- add 1–2 reps,
- add a set,
- add a little weight (e.g., 1–2.5 kg),
- slow the tempo, or
- choose a harder variation (e.g., knee push-up → full push-up).

Keep a **training log**.

steps.title: Reps, sets and rest
steps.body:
- **Strength**: roughly 3–6 reps per set with heavier loads, longer rest (2–3 min).
- **Muscle growth (hypertrophy)**: roughly 6–12+ reps, 1–2 min rest.
- **Muscular endurance**: 12–20+ reps, shorter rest.

Beginners do well with **2–3 sets of 8–12 reps**, finishing each set with **1–3 reps 'in reserve'** (you could do a couple more with good form). Train each major muscle group **2–3 times a week**, with a rest day between hard sessions for the same muscles.

steps.title: Breathing and bracing
steps.body:
- Generally, **breathe out on the effort** (standing up from a squat, pushing up), breathe in on the easier phase.
- For heavier lifts, experienced lifters 'brace' the trunk by taking a breath and tightening the core. Holding the breath hard (the Valsalva manoeuvre) raises blood pressure sharply — **people with high blood pressure, heart or eye conditions should avoid breath-holding** and lift lighter loads while breathing continuously.

steps.title: Is strength training safe for teens?
steps.body: Many expert bodies agree that **properly supervised, well-designed** resistance training is safe and beneficial for children and teenagers — improving strength, bone health and sports performance. The keys are **qualified supervision, technique first, gradual progression** and avoiding maximal lifts with poor form. It doesn't 'stunt growth'.

quiz.why: Small, steady increases drive adaptation.

quiz.why: Expert consensus supports supervised youth resistance training.

lessons.title: Lower body: squat and lunge

scenes.text: Mr. Banerjee, 52, from Kolkata, struggles to get up from low chairs.
His daughter, a physiotherapy student, starts him on 'chair squats' — sit down slowly, stand up.
He does 3 sets of 10, three days a week, adding a water bottle in each hand later.
Two months on, he gets up from the floor after playing with his grandson without help.

steps.title: The bodyweight squat, step by step
steps.body:
1. Stand with feet about **shoulder-width**, toes turned out slightly (about 10–30°).
2. Brace your trunk gently; chest proud, eyes forward.
3. **Push the hips back and bend the knees** together, as if sitting into a chair.
4. Keep **knees tracking over the toes** (in line with your middle toes) — don't let them cave inwards.
5. Keep **heels down**, weight across the whole foot.
6. Go as deep as you can with a **neutral spine** (thighs parallel or comfortable depth).
7. **Drive up** through the whole foot, breathing out.

steps.title: Common squat mistakes
steps.body:
- **Knees caving in** (valgus) → cue 'push the knees out over the toes'.
- **Heels lifting** → weight too far forward; widen stance, sit back, or work on ankle mobility.
- **Rounding the lower back** at the bottom → reduce depth.
- Knees going past the toes is **normal** for many people — what matters is control and alignment.

steps.title: The lunge
steps.body:
- **Reverse lunge** (easier on knees): step one foot back, lower until both knees are about 90°, front knee over the ankle/mid-foot, torso tall. Push through the front heel to return.
- **Forward lunge**: step forward; same alignment.
- **Split squat**: feet stay in place; go up and down.
- Keep the front knee tracking over the toes and hips square.

steps.title: Progressions
steps.body:
Chair squat (sit to stand) → bodyweight squat → goblet squat (holding a weight at the chest) → barbell squat with a coach.

Split squat with support → reverse lunge → walking lunge → loaded lunges.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do 3 sets of 10 chair squats: sit down slowly (3 seconds), stand up (1 second). If it's easy, move to free squats. Film yourself from the front to check that your knees track over your toes.

lessons.title: Hip hinge and pulling: deadlift pattern and rows

scenes.text: Shalini, 38, from Bengaluru, hurt her back lifting a heavy box with a rounded spine.
Once her doctor cleared her, her physio taught her the 'hip hinge' with a broomstick on her back.
She learns to bend from the hips, keep her back flat and lift with her legs and hips.
Now she does Romanian deadlifts with light dumbbells — and lifts groceries without fear.

steps.title: The hip hinge
steps.body:
The hinge is the pattern for deadlifts, kettlebell swings and safely lifting things from the floor.

1. Stand tall, feet hip-width, soft knees.
2. **Push your hips back** as if closing a car door with your bottom.
3. Torso tips forward with a **neutral (flat) spine**; knees bend only slightly.
4. Feel a stretch in the **hamstrings**.
5. **Drive the hips forward** to stand tall, squeezing the glutes.

**Broomstick check**: hold a stick along your back touching your head, upper back and tailbone. If any point loses contact, you're rounding or arching.

steps.title: Romanian deadlift (RDL) with light weights
steps.body: Hold dumbbells (or water bottles) in front of the thighs. Hinge, sliding the weights down close to the legs to just below the knees (or as far as your flat back allows), then stand up by driving the hips forward. 2–3 sets of 8–10. Keep the weights **close to your body**.

steps.title: Rows: pulling for posture
steps.body:
- **One-arm dumbbell row**: one hand and knee on a bench (or hand on a table), back flat; pull the weight towards your hip, elbow close to the body, squeeze the shoulder blade back; lower slowly.
- **Inverted row**: lie under a sturdy table, grip the edge, body straight, pull your chest up.
- **Band row**: anchor a band, pull handles to your ribs.

Pulling balances all the pushing we do and helps posture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Rounding the back** under load — the classic cause of strain.
- Turning the hinge into a squat (too much knee bend).
- Jerking the weight up.
- Shrugging shoulders to the ears during rows.

Back pain that radiates down the leg, numbness, or loss of bladder/bowel control → **see a doctor urgently**.

lessons.title: Upper body push and core: push-ups, planks and more

scenes.text: Tara, 16, from Shimla, can't do a single push-up and feels embarrassed in PE.
Her PE teacher starts her on wall push-ups, then push-ups with hands on a bench.
She lowers the bench height every two weeks.
By the end of term she does 10 full push-ups with a straight body.

steps.title: The push-up
steps.body:
1. Hands slightly wider than shoulders, under or just outside the chest.
2. Body in a **straight line** from head to heels — squeeze glutes, brace the abs.
3. Lower the chest towards the floor, **elbows about 45°** from the body (not flared straight out).
4. Push the floor away; breathe out.

**Progressions**: wall push-up → incline (hands on a table/bench) → knee push-up → full push-up → feet elevated.

steps.title: Core: plank, side plank, dead bug, bird dog
steps.body:
- **Plank**: forearms under shoulders, straight line, don't let hips sag or pike. Start with 20–30 s.
- **Side plank**: elbow under shoulder, hips lifted, body straight. Knees bent to make it easier.
- **Dead bug**: on your back, arms up, knees at 90°; slowly extend opposite arm and leg while keeping the lower back gently pressed down.
- **Bird dog**: on hands and knees, extend opposite arm and leg, keep hips level.

The core's job is mostly to **resist** movement and keep the spine stable.

steps.title: Overhead and shoulder care
steps.body:
- **Overhead press** (dumbbells or bottles): brace, press straight up without arching the lower back.
- **Wall slides** and **band external rotations** keep shoulders healthy.
- If overhead movements cause pain, stop and get assessed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hips sagging in push-ups or planks → lower-back strain.
- Elbows flared to 90° → shoulder stress.
- Holding planks for minutes with poor form — better short and perfect.
- Crunching hundreds of sit-ups expecting belly fat to disappear — **spot reduction doesn't work**.

quiz.why: About 45° protects the shoulders.

quiz.why: Anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral flexion.

quiz.why: Fat loss happens across the whole body.

lessons.title: Home workouts: a 3-day plan with no equipment

story.title: The mother of two in Patna

scenes.text: Rekha, 33, from Patna, has two small children and no time for a gym.
She sets a 25-minute timer three mornings a week while the children have breakfast.
Sometimes her daughter copies her squats — it becomes family fun.
After three months she's stronger, sleeping better and more confident.

steps.title: The plan (3 non-consecutive days)
steps.body:
**Warm-up (5 min)**: march, arm circles, hip circles, 10 slow squats.

**Circuit** — do 2–3 rounds, 45 s work / 15 s rest (or 10–12 reps):
- Squat (or chair squat)
- Incline or knee push-up
- Glute bridge
- Reverse lunge (alternating)
- Row with a backpack or bottle (each arm)
- Plank or dead bug

**Cool-down (5 min)**: walk around, stretch hamstrings, hips, chest, calves.

steps.title: Household 'equipment'
steps.body:
- **Backpack** with books: add load to squats, rows and lunges.
- **Water bottles** (1–2 L): light dumbbells.
- **Sturdy chair or step**: incline push-ups, step-ups, triceps dips (only if your shoulders are healthy).
- **Towel**: sliding on smooth floors, stretching.

Check that furniture is stable and the floor isn't slippery.

steps.title: How to progress
steps.body: Each week, choose **one**: add a round, add 2–3 reps, add a little load (heavier backpack), or move to a harder variation. Every 4–6 weeks, take an easier week to recover.

steps.title: Staying consistent
steps.body:
- Same time, same place: link it to a habit (after brushing teeth).
- Track sessions on a calendar.
- If you miss a day, just do the next one — no guilt spiral.
- Something is better than nothing: 10 minutes still counts.

lessons.title: Flexibility and mobility

scenes.text: Prakash, 44, an accountant in Ahmedabad, sits 10 hours a day. He can't touch his knees, let alone his toes.
He starts 10 minutes of stretching every evening after work.
He measures his sit-and-reach every month.
After three months, his back feels better and he can tie his shoelaces standing on one leg.

steps.title: Flexibility vs mobility
steps.body:
- **Flexibility**: how far a muscle can lengthen (passive range).
- **Mobility**: how well you can **actively control** a joint through its range.

Both matter; strength through a full range (e.g., deep squats) builds mobility.

steps.title: Types of stretching
steps.body:
- **Static**: hold a gentle stretch **20–30 seconds** (older adults may benefit from 30–60 s), 2–4 times. Best after exercise or as a separate session.
- **Dynamic**: controlled movements through range (leg swings, walking lunges) — best in warm-ups.
- **PNF (contract–relax)**: stretch, contract the muscle against resistance for a few seconds, relax and stretch further — effective, best learned with a coach or physio.
- **Ballistic** (bouncing): for specific trained athletes only.

Flexibility improves with regular practice — aim for **2–3 or more days a week**.

steps.title: A 10-minute evening routine
steps.body:
Hold each 30 seconds, both sides where relevant:
- Standing calf stretch against a wall
- Hamstring stretch (one heel on a low step, hinge forward with a flat back)
- Kneeling hip-flexor stretch
- Figure-4 glute stretch (lying)
- Doorway chest stretch
- Child's pose / gentle back stretch
- Neck side bends (gentle)

steps.title: Safety and mistakes
steps.body:
- Stretch to **mild tension**, never pain.
- Don't bounce in static stretches.
- Breathe slowly; don't hold your breath.
- If you have joint hypermobility, recent surgery, osteoporosis or a joint replacement, ask your doctor or physio which stretches are safe.

lessons.title: Injury prevention and first steps after an injury

story.title: The rolled ankle at the turf

scenes.text: Ali, 22, rolls his ankle during five-a-side football on a turf in Hyderabad.
His friend wants to massage it hard and tell him to 'walk it off'.
Another friend, a physio student, remembers PEACE & LOVE: protect, elevate, compress, educate — then gradual loading.
Ali can bear weight and walk four steps, so they skip the hospital that night but see a doctor next day. He returns in three weeks with a balance programme.

steps.title: Preventing injuries
steps.body:
- **Warm up** properly (RAMP).
- **Progress gradually**: big sudden jumps in training load are a key cause of overuse injuries.
- **Strength training** — especially hips, hamstrings, calves, core and shoulders.
- **Balance training** (single-leg exercises) reduces ankle sprains.
- **Rest and sleep**; don't train hard when ill.
- **Right equipment**: proper shoes, shin guards, helmets.
- **Technique**: learn safe landing, lifting and throwing.

steps.title: Soreness or injury?
steps.body:
**Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)**: dull, general muscle ache, starts 12–24 h after unaccustomed exercise, peaks around 24–72 h, eases with gentle movement. Normal.

**Possible injury**: sharp or sudden pain, pain in a joint, swelling, bruising, pain that gets worse with activity, limping, can't bear weight, pain at night, numbness or tingling, or pain that lasts more than a few days. → Stop and get assessed.

steps.title: PEACE & LOVE (soft-tissue injuries)
steps.body:
Published in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine* (2019) as an update to RICE:

**First days — PEACE**
- **P**rotect: reduce movement that causes pain for 1–3 days.
- **E**levate: raise the limb above the heart when possible.
- **A**void anti-inflammatories (and lots of ice) early, as they may interfere with healing — follow your doctor's advice.
- **C**ompress: a bandage or taping to reduce swelling.
- **E**ducate: understand that active recovery usually beats passive treatment.

**After the first days — LOVE**
- **L**oad: let pain guide a gradual return to normal activity.
- **O**ptimism: confidence helps recovery.
- **V**ascularisation: pain-free cardio to boost blood flow.
- **E**xercise: restore strength, mobility and balance.

steps.title: When to see a doctor (or call 112)
steps.body:
- Can't bear weight or take four steps, or obvious deformity → **urgent medical care** (possible fracture).
- Head injury with confusion, vomiting or loss of consciousness → **112**.
- Chest pain, fainting or collapse during exercise → **112**; start CPR if the person isn't breathing normally.
- Numbness, severe swelling, or pain not improving in a few days → see a doctor or physiotherapist.

General education, not medical advice.

lessons.title: Fitness for seniors: balance, strength and falls prevention

scenes.text: Kamala, 72, from Madurai, had a fall last year and now fears walking to the temple alone.
At her community centre, a volunteer leads a gentle chair-and-balance class twice a week.
She practises sit-to-stand, heel raises and heel-to-toe walking holding the kitchen counter at home.
Six months later she walks to the temple confidently — and has joined a laughter yoga group.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: General education, not medical advice. Older adults — especially those with heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, osteoporosis, joint replacements, dizziness or previous falls — should **check with their doctor** before starting a new programme. Exercise near a sturdy support (counter, chair back, wall). Stop for chest pain, dizziness or severe breathlessness and seek help (**112**).

steps.title: Why balance and strength matter
steps.body: With age we lose muscle and power unless we use them. Weak legs and poor balance are major causes of **falls**, which can lead to fractures and loss of independence. WHO recommends older adults do varied activities emphasising **balance and strength** on **3 or more days a week**, alongside aerobic activity. Programmes combining balance and strength exercise have been shown to reduce falls.

steps.title: A 20-minute routine
steps.body:
Warm up: march in place holding a chair, shoulder rolls (3 min).

- **Sit-to-stand** from a firm chair: 2 × 8–10 (use hands at first).
- **Heel raises** holding a counter: 2 × 10.
- **Side leg raises** holding a chair: 2 × 8 each side.
- **Standing on one leg** holding the counter, 10–30 s each side.
- **Heel-to-toe walk** along the counter: 10 steps, 2–3 times.
- **Wall push-ups**: 2 × 8–10.
- **Seated marching** and ankle circles.

Cool down: gentle stretches for calves, chest and shoulders.

steps.title: Other great choices
steps.body:
- **Walking** — build up gradually.
- **Tai chi** — shown to improve balance and reduce falls.
- **Gentle yoga** (with modifications, avoiding extreme forward bends if you have osteoporosis).
- **Water exercise** — easy on the joints.
- Social classes improve motivation and mood too.

steps.title: Falls-proof the home
steps.body:
- Good lighting, especially at night on the way to the bathroom.
- Remove loose rugs and clutter; use non-slip mats in bathrooms.
- Grab rails near toilet and shower.
- Well-fitting, non-slip footwear.
- Regular eye checks and medicine reviews (some medicines cause dizziness).

lessons.title: Coaching others: screening, cueing and progressions (for would-be trainers)

scenes.text: Joseph, 23, from Kochi, has just started as a junior trainer at a neighbourhood gym.
His first client, Mrs. D'Souza, 58, wants to 'get fit fast'. Joseph almost puts her straight on a hard circuit.
His senior trainer stops him: 'Screen first. Ask about health. Start where she is.'
Joseph's careful plan keeps her safe; a year later she is still training and refers four friends.

steps.title: Screening before exercise
steps.body:
- Use a pre-activity questionnaire such as the **PAR-Q+** to ask about heart conditions, chest pain, dizziness, bone or joint problems, medicines and pregnancy.
- Ask about goals, past injuries, activity history and lifestyle.
- If there are **red flags** (e.g., chest pain, fainting, uncontrolled blood pressure or diabetes, recent surgery), **refer to a doctor** for clearance before training.
- Record everything, and re-check periodically.

steps.title: Cueing well
steps.body:
- **One cue at a time**, short and clear: 'Hips back', 'Knees out', 'Chest proud'.
- **External cues** (focus on the effect: 'push the floor away') often work better than internal ones ('contract your triceps').
- **Demonstrate**, let them try, then give feedback — positive first, then one correction.
- **Watch from the right angle**: side view for depth and back angle, front view for knee alignment.

steps.title: Regressions and progressions
steps.body:
Every exercise needs an **easier** and a **harder** version so you can meet the client where they are:

- Squat: chair sit-to-stand ← squat → goblet squat.
- Push-up: wall/incline ← knee push-up → full push-up.
- Plank: on knees ← full plank → plank with shoulder taps.

Change **one variable** at a time and observe the result.

steps.title: Scope of practice and ethics
steps.body:
- Fitness trainers **don't diagnose injuries, treat medical conditions or prescribe diets for diseases** — refer to doctors, physiotherapists and registered dietitians.
- **Never recommend banned substances** or unregulated supplements.
- Respect consent: explain and ask before touching to correct form.
- Keep client information private.
- Learn first aid and CPR; know the gym's emergency plan.

Coaching qualifications (e.g., NIS sports coaching courses or accredited fitness certifications) build credibility.

lessons.title: The ground, the pitch and the players

scenes.text: Aarav, 9, has played gully cricket in his lane in Pune for years — one tip one hand, the wall is the wicket keeper.
His school coach, Ms. Fernandes, takes the class to a real ground. Aarav is amazed: a huge oval, a white rope, and in the middle a hard strip of rolled earth with white lines.
'Why are there two sets of stumps? Why is that line painted there? Where do I stand?' he asks.
Ms. Fernandes smiles: 'Let's walk the ground. Once you know the map, the game makes sense.'

steps.title: The field and the boundary
steps.body:
Cricket is played on a large, roughly oval field. The edge is marked by a **boundary** — usually a rope or painted line.

In the centre is the **pitch**, a strip of short, hard, rolled grass and soil. Almost all the action starts here: the bowler bowls from one end, the batter stands at the other.

Because fields differ in size, the same shot might be a four on a small ground and a catch on a big one. Good players learn the size of each ground.

steps.title: The pitch in numbers
steps.body:
- The pitch is **22 yards (20.12 m)** long between the two sets of stumps and **10 feet (3.05 m)** wide.
- At each end stands a **wicket**: three **stumps** with two **bails** resting on top.
- The **popping crease** (the batting crease) is a line 4 feet (1.22 m) in front of the stumps. A batter is 'in their ground' when bat or body is grounded behind it.
- The **bowling crease** runs through the stumps; the **return creases** run at right angles at the sides and mark how wide the bowler may go.

Try this: pace out 22 yards in your lane — about 20 big steps for an adult. That's how far a ball travels from the bowler's hand.

steps.title: Who is on the field
steps.body:
Each team has **11 players**.

- The **batting side** has only **two batters** on the field at a time: the **striker** (facing the bowler) and the **non-striker** (at the bowler's end, ready to run).
- The **fielding side** has all 11 on the field: one **bowler**, one **wicket-keeper** (the only fielder allowed to wear gloves and leg guards), and nine other fielders.
- Two **on-field umpires** make decisions; in big matches a **third umpire** watches video replays and a **match referee** looks after discipline.

The captain of the fielding side decides who bowls and where fielders stand.

steps.title: Formats: Test, ODI, T20
steps.body:
The same Laws apply, but matches come in different lengths:

- **Test cricket**: up to five days, each team bats twice (two innings each). The red ball and white clothes are traditional.
- **One-Day International (ODI)**: each side bats once for up to **50 overs**.
- **T20**: each side bats once for up to **20 overs** — fast, explosive, used in leagues like the IPL and WPL.

School and club cricket often uses shorter formats (for example 20 or 30 overs) to fit the day.

steps.title: Safety with a hard ball
steps.body:
A cricket ball is hard (about 156–163 g for men's senior cricket, lighter for juniors and women's cricket). When you move from a tennis ball to a leather ball:

- Always wear a **helmet**, pads, gloves and an abdominal guard when batting, and a helmet when keeping close or fielding very close to the bat.
- Never walk behind a batter who is practising swings, or in front of a net where someone is bowling.
- Juniors should use the right-sized bat and ball for their age.

steps.title: Common beginner mix-ups
steps.body:
- 'Wicket' can mean the stumps, the pitch ('a flat wicket') or a dismissal ('he took a wicket'). Context tells you which.
- 'Batsman/batter': the Laws now use the gender-neutral **batter**.
- An **innings** is always written with an s, even for one: 'one innings, two innings'.

lessons.title: How runs are scored (and what extras are)

scenes.text: Diya, 11, from Kolkata, is too injured to play this week, so her coach hands her the scorebook.
First over: the bowler bowls a ball too wide, then the batters run three, then a ball hits the batter's pad and they run one. 'Who gets which runs?' she panics.
The umpire's signals and a patient senior help her. By the end of the innings, Diya's total matches the scoreboard exactly.
'Scoring makes you understand the game better than playing,' the senior tells her.

steps.title: Runs off the bat
steps.body:
When the striker hits the ball, the two batters can **run** between the wickets. Each time both batters cross and reach the other popping crease, **one run** is scored. They can run 1, 2, 3 or more.

If the ball reaches the boundary:
- It **touches the ground** first, then crosses or touches the boundary → **4 runs**.
- It crosses the boundary **without touching the ground** (on the full) → **6 runs**.

Runs made off the bat belong to the batter's personal score and the team total.

steps.title: Extras: runs not made by the bat
steps.body:
Some runs go to the team total but not to the batter. These are **extras**:

- **Wide**: the ball is too wide of the batter to hit from a normal batting position. One run is added, and the ball must be bowled again.
- **No-ball**: an illegal delivery — most often the bowler's front foot lands fully beyond the popping crease, or a full toss passes above waist height. One run is added and the ball is bowled again. Any runs the batter hits off it also count.
- **Bye**: the ball misses bat and body and the batters run.
- **Leg-bye**: the ball hits the batter's body (not the bat or the glove holding it) and the batters run — but only if the batter tried to play a shot or tried to get out of the way.
- **Penalty runs**: five runs, for example when the ball hits a fielder's helmet lying on the ground.

steps.title: Worked example: one over
steps.body:
Ball 1: dot ball (no run). Ball 2: wide → team +1, ball re-bowled. Ball 2 again: batter drives for 4 → batter +4. Ball 3: batters run 2 leg-byes → team +2 (not the batter). Ball 4: no-ball, batter hits it for 1 run → team +1 (no-ball) +1 (run) = +2, batter +1. Ball 4 again: six! Ball 5: dot. Ball 6: single.

Team total for the over: 0+1+4+2+2+6+0+1 = **16 runs**. The bowler bowled **8 deliveries** but only 6 counted as legal balls.

steps.title: The free hit
steps.body: In ODIs, T20 internationals and most T20 leagues, the delivery after a no-ball is a **free hit**. On a free hit the batter cannot be out in most ways (not bowled, caught or LBW) — but can still be **run out**. Fielders cannot change positions for a free hit unless the batters change ends.

steps.title: Common mistakes in scoring
steps.body:
- Giving leg-byes to the batter — they are extras.
- Forgetting that a wide or no-ball does not count as one of the six balls.
- Writing 'caught' when the fielder was touching the boundary rope while holding the ball — that is **not out**; it counts as a boundary (six if the ball had not bounced).

Try this: watch two overs of any match and keep your own tally of runs and extras.

lessons.title: How a batter gets out (including LBW, simply)

story.title: Kabir and the argument at the nets

scenes.text: In a club game in Bengaluru, Kabir, 13, is given LBW. 'It hit my pad outside the line!' he grumbles.
After the match, the umpire, Mr. Rao, takes him aside with a stump and a ball and walks him through the LBW Law slowly.
Kabir realises he had not offered a shot — which changes the rule about where the ball hits the pad.
Next week Kabir shakes the umpire's hand. 'Knowing the Law made me a better batter,' he says.

steps.title: The common ways out
steps.body:
- **Bowled**: the ball, bowled legally, hits the stumps and knocks off at least one bail (even if it touches bat or body first).
- **Caught**: a fielder catches the ball before it touches the ground, after it hit the bat or the glove holding the bat.
- **LBW (leg before wicket)**: the ball would have hit the stumps but hit the batter's body first (see the next step).
- **Run out**: while the batters are running, a fielder breaks the wicket and the batter is outside their ground.
- **Stumped**: the batter steps out of the crease (not trying to run), misses the ball, and the keeper breaks the wicket.

steps.title: LBW in plain words
steps.body:
For LBW, **all** of these must be true:

- The delivery is legal (not a no-ball).
- The ball did **not pitch outside the line of leg stump**.
- The ball hit the batter's body (not the bat first).
- The point of impact was **in line with the stumps** — OR it was outside off stump **and the batter made no genuine attempt to play the ball**.
- The ball **would have gone on to hit the stumps**.

In top cricket, DRS uses ball-tracking to check these, but the logic is the same.

steps.title: The rare ways out
steps.body:
- **Hit wicket**: the batter breaks their own wicket with bat or body while playing a shot or setting off for the first run.
- **Hit the ball twice**: deliberately striking it again (except to protect the stumps).
- **Obstructing the field**: deliberately blocking a fielder by word or action (handling the ball on purpose now falls here since the 2017 Laws).
- **Timed out**: a new batter not ready to face within the time allowed (3 minutes under the Laws; less in many playing conditions).
- **Retired out**: a batter leaves without the umpire's consent and without illness or injury.

Running out the non-striker who leaves the crease early before the bowler releases the ball is now covered under **run out** in the Laws (moved there in 2022).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1. A leg-spinner's ball pitches outside leg stump, spins in and hits the pad in line. **Not out** — it pitched outside leg.
2. A ball pitches on off stump, hits the pad outside off while the batter shoulders arms (no shot), and would hit the stumps. **Out** — no shot offered, so impact outside off is allowed.
3. The ball nicks the bat, hits the pad and lobs to gully who catches it. **Out caught** — it hit the bat first.
4. A no-ball hits the stumps. **Not out** — you can't be bowled off a no-ball.

steps.title: Fair play when you're out
steps.body: When the umpire raises the finger, walk off calmly. Arguing, throwing your bat or swearing can bring penalties under the Code of Conduct. If you think a decision was wrong, discuss it later with your coach — and use it to learn.

a.text: You are umpiring a school match. An off-spinner bowls; the ball pitches on middle stump, the batter pads up without playing a shot, and the ball hits the pad just outside off stump. Ball-tracking (in your head!) says it would hit off stump. What do you decide?

choices.label: Out LBW
choices.feedback: Correct reasoning: no shot offered, so impact outside off does not save the batter.

choices.label: Not out: impact was outside off
choices.feedback: That rule only protects a batter who genuinely tried to play the ball.

b.text: Next ball, the batter edges onto the pad, and the ball pops to short leg, who catches it before it touches the ground. Out or not out?

choices.label: Out caught
choices.feedback: Yes — bat first, then pad, then caught cleanly.

choices.label: Not out: it hit the pad
choices.feedback: Touching the pad after the bat doesn't stop it being a catch.

c.text: Re-think: the batter did not try to hit the ball. Under the Law, impact outside off counts in that case. Do you change your mind?

choices.label: Yes, out LBW
choices.feedback: Good — umpires must know the exact Law.

end1.text: Two correct decisions! You applied the LBW and catching Laws exactly. Great umpiring.

end2.text: Review the 'Caught' rule: a catch is fair if the ball touched bat (or glove on bat) and was caught before touching the ground — touching the pad along the way doesn't matter.

quiz.q: A ball pitches outside leg stump and would hit the stumps. Can it be LBW?
options: Only if no shot is offered
quiz.why: A ball pitching outside the line of leg stump can never give an LBW decision.

quiz.q: Can a batter be bowled off a no-ball?
quiz.why: You cannot be bowled, caught, LBW or stumped off a no-ball.

quiz.q: Which dismissal happens when the keeper breaks the wicket while the batter is out of the crease and NOT attempting a run?
quiz.why: That is stumped. If the batter was attempting a run, it would be a run out.

quiz.q: Deliberately handling the ball is now covered under which dismissal?
quiz.why: Since the 2017 Laws, 'handled the ball' was merged into obstructing the field.

quiz.q: For LBW when the impact is outside the line of off stump, which must also be true?
options: The batter made no genuine attempt to play the ball
It was the last ball of the over
quiz.why: Impact outside off only counts if the batter offered no genuine shot.

lessons.title: Overs, results, signals and the Spirit of Cricket

scenes.text: Meher, 12, from Jaipur, wants to umpire her younger brother's under-10 games.
She practises in front of the mirror: one arm out for a no-ball, both arms out for a wide, arms waving for four.
In her first match, she calmly signals a six and the scorers wave back. Both teams thank her.
At the end she leads the handshakes — her coach says that's the Spirit of Cricket in action.

steps.title: Overs and bowlers
steps.body:
- An over is **six legal deliveries** from one end; then the next over is bowled from the other end by a different bowler.
- A bowler **cannot bowl two overs in a row**.
- In ODIs a bowler may bowl at most **10 overs**; in T20s at most **4 overs**.
- **Powerplays** in limited-overs cricket restrict how many fielders may stand outside the inner circle (in ODIs during the first 10 overs and in T20Is during the first 6, only two fielders may be outside it).

steps.title: How results work
steps.body:
- In limited-overs cricket, the team with more runs wins. If the chasing team passes the target, they win 'by X wickets'; if the team batting first defends, they win 'by X runs'.
- In Tests, a team must bowl the opponent out twice and score more runs to win; if time runs out, it's a **draw**. A **tie** (equal scores, all out at the end) is very rare.
- Rain-shortened limited-overs games use the **DLS method** to set fair revised targets.
- T20 ties are often decided by a **Super Over**.

steps.title: Umpire signals you must know
steps.body:
- **Out**: index finger raised above the head.
- **Four**: arm waved side to side, finishing across the chest.
- **Six**: both arms raised straight above the head.
- **Wide**: both arms stretched out horizontally.
- **No-ball**: one arm stretched out horizontally.
- **Bye**: an open hand raised above the head.
- **Leg-bye**: touching a raised knee with the hand.
- **Dead ball**: crossing and re-crossing the wrists below the waist.
- **Short run**: bending one arm up and touching the shoulder with the fingertips.

steps.title: The Spirit of Cricket
steps.body:
The Laws begin with a preamble called the **Spirit of Cricket**: respect for your captain, team-mates, opponents and umpires, and playing hard but fair. Examples:

- Accept the umpire's decision, even when you disagree.
- Applaud a good shot or catch by the opposition.
- No abusive language, no time-wasting, no damaging the ball or pitch.
- Captains are responsible for their team's behaviour.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Stand in front of a mirror and practise every signal in the list until you can do each one in under a second without thinking. Then ask a friend to call random events ('wide!', 'leg-bye!') while you signal.

activity.prompt: Match the umpire signal to its meaning.
pairs: Arm waved side to side across chest

quiz.q: Can a bowler bowl two consecutive overs?
quiz.why: A bowler may not bowl two overs in a row.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of overs one bowler can bowl in a T20?
quiz.why: Each bowler may bowl up to 4 of the 20 overs.

quiz.q: Both arms raised straight above the head means…
quiz.why: Both arms raised high is the six signal.

quiz.q: What method sets revised targets in rain-hit limited-overs games?
quiz.why: DLS (Duckworth–Lewis–Stern) adjusts targets. DRS is the review system.

quiz.q: Which is an example of the Spirit of Cricket?
quiz.why: Respecting opponents is at the heart of the Spirit of Cricket. Saliva on the ball is banned in international cricket.

sources: MCC Laws of Cricket — Preamble and Law 2

questions.q: How many players are in a cricket team?
A ball clears the boundary without bouncing. Runs scored?
questions.why: On the full over the boundary is six.

questions.q: How many legal balls in an over?
Which umpire signal shows a wide?
questions.why: Both arms horizontal is a wide; one arm is a no-ball.

questions.q: Runs from byes are credited to…
What is the distance between the popping crease and the bowling crease?
questions.why: The popping crease is 4 feet (1.22 m) in front of the bowling crease.

questions.q: A batter, not attempting a run, steps out, misses, and the keeper removes the bails. The dismissal is…
questions.why: Stumped needs the batter out of ground and not attempting a run.

questions.q: On a free hit, which dismissal still counts?
questions.why: Run out remains possible on a free hit.

questions.q: In an ODI powerplay in the first 10 overs, how many fielders may be outside the inner circle?
questions.why: Only two fielders may be outside the circle in the first powerplay.

questions.q: A ball pitches in line, hits the pad outside off stump while the batter plays a genuine shot, and would hit the stumps. Decision?
options: Out if it was a full toss
questions.why: With a genuine shot, impact outside off is not out.

questions.q: A team batting second passes the target with 4 wickets in hand. The result is written as…
questions.why: A successful chase is recorded by wickets remaining.

questions.why: In 2022 the MCC moved it into Law 38, Run out.

options: Not out — it hit the bat
questions.why: Bowled includes the ball touching bat or body before hitting the stumps.

courses.title: Batting technique: grip, stance, footwork, drives and the pull
courses.summary: A complete batting foundation: how to hold the bat, stand, pick up the bat, move your feet, play the front-foot drives, the back-foot pull and cut, and run between the wickets — with drills you can do at home or in the nets.

lessons.title: Grip, stance and guard

scenes.text: Rohan, 12, from a village near Indore, hits the ball hard but it keeps flying to the leg side or straight up.
His academy coach, Mr. Siddiqui, watches one ball and says, 'Show me your hands.' Rohan's bottom hand is wrapped round the back of the handle.
They fix the grip and stance for 20 minutes with no ball at all — just shadow batting in front of a mirror.
Next session, Rohan drives straight back past the bowler for the first time. 'It all starts with the hands,' says the coach.

steps.title: The grip, step by step
steps.body:
For a right-handed batter (mirror everything if you are left-handed):

- Lay the bat face-down on the ground, handle towards you.
- Pick it up with both hands **close together** near the top of the handle — left hand on top, right hand just below.
- The 'V' shapes made by your thumb and first finger of **both hands should line up**, pointing roughly down the middle of the back of the bat, between the splice and the outside edge.
- Grip **firmly but not tightly** — imagine holding a bird: firm enough it can't escape, soft enough not to hurt it. Tension in the hands kills timing.

The **top hand** guides the bat and keeps the face straight; the **bottom hand** adds power. Many coaching manuals describe the bottom hand as being held with the thumb and first finger, lighter than the top hand.

steps.title: Common grip mistakes
steps.body:
- **Bottom hand too far round** the back of the handle: the bat face closes and the ball goes to leg or in the air.
- **Hands far apart**: you lose control and can't play straight.
- **Death grip**: white knuckles = stiff arms and no timing.
- **Bottom hand too strong** on defensive shots: the ball pops up for a catch.

steps.title: The stance
steps.body:
- Stand **side-on**, feet about shoulder-width apart, either side of the popping crease, parallel to it.
- Knees **slightly flexed**, weight on the **balls of the feet** and spread evenly.
- Front shoulder points down the pitch towards the bowler.
- **Head still, eyes level**, looking at the bowler over the front shoulder. Both eyes should see the bowler.
- Bat rests near the back toe, hands relaxed near the front thigh.

A good stance is **balanced and comfortable** — you should be able to move forward or back equally easily.

steps.title: Taking guard
steps.body:
Before facing, you ask the umpire for a **guard** — a mark showing where your bat rests relative to the stumps behind you:

- **Middle** (centre): good all-round choice.
- **Leg stump**: gives room to hit through the off side.
- **Middle-and-leg**: a common compromise.

Hold the bat upright on the crease and the umpire tells you 'a bit towards you / away' until it's lined up. Scratch a mark with your studs or bat.

steps.title: Try this at home
steps.body: Shadow-bat in front of a mirror for 5 minutes a day: grip check, stance, head still, eyes level. Freeze and check: Are your Vs lined up? Is your weight balanced? Can you lift one foot without wobbling? Ask someone to film you from side-on and from the bowler's view.

activity.prompt: Daily grip & stance drill (no ball needed). Tick each when done.
items: Pick up the bat from face-down and check both Vs line up
Hold the grip relaxed for 30 seconds — no white knuckles
Take stance: feet shoulder-width, knees soft, weight on balls of feet
Check head still and eyes level in a mirror
Hold the stance 10 seconds, then step forward and back without losing balance — 10 times
Film yourself once and compare to a coach or a good player's stance

quiz.q: For a right-hander, which hand goes on top of the handle?
quiz.why: The left (top) hand is on top and guides the bat face for a right-hander.

quiz.q: The Vs of thumb and first finger should be…
quiz.why: Aligned Vs keep the bat face square.

quiz.q: Where should your weight be in the stance?
options: On the balls of the feet, evenly spread
quiz.why: Balanced on the balls of the feet lets you move either way quickly.

quiz.q: What happens if the bottom hand is wrapped too far round?
options: The bat face closes and the ball goes to leg or in the air
quiz.why: A strong bottom hand closes the face.

quiz.q: Why keep eyes level?
options: Helps judge line and length accurately
quiz.why: Level eyes give the brain the most accurate picture of the ball.

lessons.title: Backlift, footwork and reading length

story.title: Ishaan is stuck on the crease

scenes.text: Ishaan, 14, in Chennai, gets out the same way every match: feet frozen, edging to slip.
Coach Lakshmi places a cone on the pitch. 'Anything pitching in front of this, go forward. Behind it, go back.'
They do 100 throw-downs where Ishaan only moves his feet — no shot, just front or back, then freeze.
A month later his feet decide before his bat does. The edges stop.

steps.title: The backlift
steps.body:
As the bowler runs in, you lift the bat back ready to play. A good **backlift**:

- Goes back roughly towards **second slip / off stump** (a straight-ish line), not wildly towards leg.
- Is led by the **top hand**, with the face slightly open.
- Is ready (bat up) by the time the ball is released.

Some batters use a higher backlift for power, others a short one for control. What matters is that the bat **comes down straight** along the line of the ball.

steps.title: Length decides your feet
steps.body:
**Length** is where the ball bounces.

- **Full** (pitches close to you): get **forward** to the pitch of the ball and smother any movement.
- **Good length** (the awkward zone): usually a decisive forward defence or a back-foot defence depending on bounce.
- **Short** (pitches well in front of you and rises): go **back** to give yourself time and play from under your eyes.

The secret is to **pick length early** — from the bowler's hand and the first part of the ball's flight — and commit. Half-forward, half-back is where edges come from.

steps.title: Front-foot and back-foot movement
steps.body:
**Front foot**: lead with the **head and front shoulder**, step the front foot towards the line of the ball, knee bent, head over or just ahead of the front knee.

**Back foot**: step **back and slightly across** towards off stump with the back foot, staying side-on for defence, so your head is in line with the ball. Your weight goes onto the back foot but you stay tall.

A small **trigger movement** (for example a little press forward or back-and-across before the ball is bowled) helps some batters move early; keep it small and finish it before release.

steps.title: Head position is everything
steps.body: Where the head goes, the body follows. If your head falls towards the off side, you'll play around your front pad and be LBW; if it falls to leg, you'll edge to slip. Coaches often say: **'Head over the ball, eyes level, still at contact.'**

steps.title: Partner drill: front or back?
steps.body: A partner throws a tennis ball from 10–12 m, mixing full and short lengths. You only move — front foot or back foot — and freeze with the bat in a defensive position. Partner shouts 'yes' if you chose right. Do sets of 12, rest, repeat 3 times. Then add the defensive shot.

activity.prompt: Front foot or back foot? Sort each ball.

items.text: A full ball pitching near your toes
A short ball rising to chest height
A slow, flighted spinner pitched up
A short, wide ball outside off stump
A bouncer aimed at your body

quiz.q: A ball pitches very close to the batter. The best foot movement is…
quiz.why: Getting forward to a full ball kills movement and lets you drive.

quiz.q: Where should the backlift generally go?
options: Towards the slips / off stump area
quiz.why: A backlift towards the slips helps the bat come down straight.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of edges?
quiz.why: Indecision in footwork causes edges.

quiz.q: On the back foot you step…
options: Back and slightly across towards off
quiz.why: Back and across gets your head in line with the ball.

lessons.title: Front-foot shots: forward defence, straight drive, cover drive, on drive

scenes.text: Ananya, 15, from Ahmedabad, dreams of playing for India like the women stars she watches on TV.
Her coach makes her play only the forward defence for a whole week. She is annoyed.
In week two the coach adds 'push a little harder' — and the defence becomes a beautiful straight drive.
In the district U-16 trial she drives the selector's first ball back past the bowler. The coach just nods.

steps.title: Forward defence: the mother of all shots
steps.body:
- Lead with the **head and front shoulder** towards the line of the ball.
- Step forward; the front foot lands close to the line of the ball, front knee bent.
- Bat comes down **straight**, close to the front pad, **angled down** (handle ahead of the blade) so the ball goes into the ground.
- Top hand in control; bottom hand loose (some coaches say just thumb and finger).
- Head over the ball, eyes on it at contact. **Hold the finish** for a second.

Goal: soft hands, ball dropping dead near your feet.

steps.title: Straight drive
steps.body:
Same set-up as the forward defence, but for a full ball you **swing through**:

- Front elbow **high**, pointing down the pitch.
- Full face of the bat presented straight back to the bowler.
- Contact under your eyes, just beside the front pad.
- **Follow through** high and straight, finishing with hands high.

Power comes from **timing and weight transfer**, not from muscle.

steps.title: Cover drive and on drive
steps.body:
**Cover drive** (full ball outside off stump): front foot steps **towards the line** outside off; head and shoulder lead; front elbow high; bat swings down and through towards cover. Keep the bat face presented to cover and finish high.

**On drive** (full ball on middle or leg stump): the front foot points slightly towards mid-on, the front shoulder 'opens' a little, but the head still leads; drive between mid-on and mid-wicket. This is one of the hardest drives — don't let the bottom hand take over.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Driving at balls that are not full** → edges to slip. Only drive when the ball is pitched up.
- **Head falling away** → bat comes across the line.
- **Big stride, no balance** → you can't adjust to swing or spin.
- **Hitting in the air** → usually the bottom hand dominating or contact in front of the pad.
- **Gap between bat and pad** → bowled 'through the gate'.

steps.title: Drill: bucket target
steps.body: Put a bucket 15 m away straight down the ground and another at cover. With a partner feeding half-volleys (underarm bounce feeds are fine), play 10 straight drives along the ground at the first bucket, then 10 cover drives. Score a point for every ball that rolls past or into the target zone **along the ground**.

activity.prompt: Put the straight drive in the correct order.
items: Pick the length early: it's full
Head and front shoulder lead towards the ball
Front foot steps to the line of the ball, knee bent
Bat comes down straight, front elbow high
Contact under the eyes beside the front pad
Follow through high and straight; hold your balance

quiz.q: In a forward defence, the bat face should be angled…
options: Down, with the handle ahead of the blade
quiz.why: Angling the bat down keeps the ball on the ground.

quiz.q: What leads the body into a front-foot shot?
quiz.why: Head and front shoulder lead; the body follows.

quiz.q: When should you play a drive?
options: Only when the ball is full / pitched up
quiz.why: Drives are for full balls; driving at short-of-length balls causes edges.

quiz.q: Being 'bowled through the gate' means…
options: Ball went between bat and pad
quiz.why: A gap between bat and pad lets the ball through onto the stumps.

quiz.q: Power in a drive mainly comes from…
quiz.why: Well-timed contact with weight moving forward produces power.

lessons.title: Back-foot shots: defence, pull and cut

story.title: Joe in Leeds and the short ball

scenes.text: Joe, 16, plays club cricket in Leeds, England. Fast bowlers keep testing him with short balls.
He keeps turning his head away. His coach, Priya, an Indian-origin former county player, stops the session.
They start with tennis balls thrown short at the body: 'Watch it, get inside the line, roll the wrists.'
By the end of the season Joe's pull shot is his best scoring shot — always with his helmet on.

steps.title: Back-foot defence
steps.body:
For a short-of-length ball rising towards the stumps or body:

- Back foot moves **back and across** towards off stump, parallel to the crease.
- Stay **tall and side-on**; front foot comes back lightly for balance.
- Top-hand elbow high, bat straight and close to the body, **played under the eyes**.
- Soft bottom hand; let the ball drop down in front of you.

steps.title: The pull shot
steps.body:
For a short ball at **waist to chest height**, usually on middle or leg stump line:

- Pick it short early. Back foot goes **back and across** (some players go back towards leg if the ball is wide of leg).
- Get your **head inside or in line** with the ball and keep your eyes on it.
- Swing the bat **horizontally**, making contact at arm's length **in front of your body**.
- **Roll the wrists** over at contact so the ball goes down, towards mid-wicket or square leg.
- Weight transfers from back foot to front foot as you rotate.

The **hook** is the same family of shot for a higher ball (head height) — far riskier. Learn to duck or sway under very high bouncers first.

steps.title: The cut shot
steps.body:
For a short ball **wide outside off stump**:

- Back foot moves **back and across** towards the line of the ball.
- Wait for the ball to come to you; strike **down** on it with a horizontal bat and straight arms.
- Aim between point and cover; roll the wrists or 'hit down' to keep it on the ground.

Cut only when there is **width and shortness**. Cutting a ball close to off stump is the classic way to edge to the keeper.

steps.title: Safety for short-ball practice
steps.body:
- **Always wear a properly fitted helmet** with a grille when facing a hard ball — in matches and nets.
- Learn the pull with **tennis or soft balls**, then progress to a bowling machine at low speed under a coach.
- Never take your eyes off the ball or turn your back — that's when people get hit.
- If you are hit on the head, stop batting and get checked: **concussion** symptoms (headache, dizziness, confusion, sickness) need medical assessment the same day. 'If in doubt, sit it out.'

steps.title: Drill: tennis-ball pull
steps.body: Partner throws a tennis ball overarm, bouncing it halfway so it reaches you at waist height. Play 10 pulls, focusing on: back-and-across, head still, contact in front, wrists roll, ball along the ground. Score 1 for every ball that stays down. Repeat with cuts for wide short balls.

statements.s: The pull shot is played to a short ball at waist to chest height.
statements.why: That's the classic pull ball. Higher balls are hooked or avoided.

statements.s: You should cut a short ball that is very close to off stump.
statements.why: Cut only with width; close to off stump the cut usually edges behind.

statements.s: Rolling the wrists helps keep the pull along the ground.
statements.why: Rolling turns the bat face down at contact.

statements.s: It's fine to face a hard ball without a helmet if you are good at ducking.
statements.why: Always wear a properly fitted helmet with a hard ball.

statements.s: Contact for the pull should be in front of the body.
statements.why: Contact in front gives control and power; late contact top-edges.

quiz.q: What is the first footwork for the pull?
options: Step to square leg and freeze
quiz.why: Back and across gets you in position and gives time.

quiz.q: The cut is played to a ball that is…
quiz.why: Cut short, wide deliveries.

quiz.q: If you are hit on the head and feel dizzy, you should…
options: Take off the helmet and carry on
quiz.why: Possible concussion needs assessment; if in doubt, sit it out.

quiz.q: Why learn the pull with tennis balls first?
options: They allow safe repetitions while learning technique
quiz.why: Soft balls let you groove technique without injury risk.

quiz.q: Where should your head be for a pull shot?
options: Inside or in line with the ball, eyes on it
quiz.why: Keeping the head in line and eyes on the ball is key to control and safety.

lessons.title: Running between wickets and building an innings

scenes.text: Twins Arjun and Arnav, 13, from Lucknow, open the batting. In one match, both run to the same end — a run-out.
They blame each other all the way home.
Their coach teaches them three words — 'Yes', 'No', 'Wait' — and who should call when.
Next season they lead the league in singles and never run each other out again.

steps.title: Calling: Yes, No, Wait
steps.body:
Calls must be **loud, clear and early**:

- **'Yes!'** — we're running.
- **'No!'** — we're not running.
- **'Wait!'** — let's see if the ball beats the fielder; follow quickly with Yes or No.

**Who calls?** A common rule: the **striker** calls when the ball goes **in front of the wicket** (they can see it); the **non-striker** calls when it goes **behind square** (the striker would have to turn). Agree this before you bat.

steps.title: Running technique
steps.body:
- **Non-striker backs up**: walk a few steps out as the bowler releases (stay in your ground until the ball is released!).
- **Run in a straight line**, slightly to the side of the pitch so you don't damage the protected area.
- **Carry the bat** in the hand nearest the side you'll turn, and **slide it in** over the popping crease — a slid bat reaches the line faster than a foot.
- **Turn facing the ball** so you can see where it is for the next run.
- First run **fast** — it creates pressure and turns ones into twos.

steps.title: Building an innings
steps.body:
- **Early**: respect good balls, leave well outside off stump, get your eye in.
- **Rotate strike**: singles keep the scoreboard moving and frustrate bowlers.
- **Set mini-targets**: e.g., the next 5 overs, or 10 runs at a time.
- **Partnerships**: talk between overs — about the pitch, the bowlers, which fielders are slow.
- **Change gear** with the match situation: in a chase, know the required run rate.

steps.title: Worked example: the required run rate
steps.body: Your team needs 72 runs from 12 overs. Required rate = 72 ÷ 12 = **6 runs per over**. If you score 4 in the next over, you need 68 from 11 = about 6.2 per over. Singles every ball would give 6 an over — so steady rotation plus one boundary every couple of overs keeps you on track.

steps.title: Common running mistakes
steps.body:
- Ball-watching while running instead of watching your partner and the line.
- A late 'Wait' that turns into 'Yes' too slowly.
- Not grounding the bat — running past the crease with the bat in the air can still be out if it's not grounded.
- Both batters looking at the ball and nobody calling.

a.text: You're the non-striker. Your partner glances the ball fine down the leg side, behind square. Who should call?

choices.label: I call — it's behind square
choices.feedback: Correct — the striker can't easily see it.

choices.label: The striker calls
choices.feedback: Usually behind square is the non-striker's call.

b.text: The fine-leg fielder is slow and far away. You call 'Yes!' and you both run one. The ball is still being picked up. What now?

choices.label: Turn facing the ball and call 'Yes' for two
choices.feedback: Turning towards the ball lets you judge the second run.

choices.label: Turn with your back to the ball and just run
choices.feedback: You can't see the throw — risky!

c.text: The striker had to turn to look, called late, and you both hesitate mid-pitch. A fielder throws. Lesson?

choices.label: Agree before batting: behind square = non-striker calls
choices.feedback: Exactly. Let's try again with a clear system.

end1.text: Two runs, safely completed. Clear calls and smart turns win matches.

end2.text: You made it, but only just. Always turn facing the ball so you can see the danger.

quiz.q: Which three calls are used in running?
quiz.why: Yes, No and Wait are standard.

quiz.q: Why slide the bat over the crease?
options: It reaches the line faster than a foot
quiz.why: A grounded, sliding bat extends your reach.

quiz.q: Need 60 off 10 overs. Required run rate?
quiz.why: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 runs per over.

quiz.q: When should the non-striker leave the crease to back up?
options: Only after the ball is released
After the ball reaches the keeper
quiz.why: Leaving before release risks being run out at the bowler's end.

questions.q: For a right-hander, which hand is on top of the bat handle?
questions.why: The left hand is the top, guiding hand.

questions.q: A good stance has weight…
options: On the balls of the feet

lessons.title: A safe, legal bowling action

scenes.text: Neha, 14, a quick bowler from Guwahati, has started getting lower-back pain after long spells.
Her coach films her from behind: her hips point one way, her shoulders another as she lands.
A sports physio explains that this 'mixed action' is linked to back stress injuries in young fast bowlers.
They work on aligning hips and shoulders and limit her overs. A year later she's quicker — and pain-free.

steps.title: What makes a delivery legal
steps.body:
- **Front foot**: when the front foot lands, **some part of it must be behind the popping crease** (it can be grounded or raised). If the whole foot is over the line → no-ball.
- **Back foot**: must land **within and not touching the return crease** on its side.
- **Arm**: the ball must be **bowled, not thrown**. ICC regulations allow up to **15 degrees** of elbow extension during delivery; more than that is an illegal action.
- You must tell the umpire which arm you bowl with and from which side of the wicket (over or round).

steps.title: The phases of the action
steps.body:
1. **Run-up**: smooth, rhythmic and repeatable; it builds speed you can control. Measure it and mark it.
2. **Gather / jump**: a small bound into the delivery stride.
3. **Back-foot contact**: body coils; front arm high, eyes on the target.
4. **Front-foot contact**: front leg braces, body rotates powerfully.
5. **Release**: bowling arm comes over high and straight, wrist behind the ball.
6. **Follow-through**: keep moving forward and then veer off the pitch so you don't damage the protected area.

Actions are often described as **side-on**, **front-on** or **semi-open**. All can be safe — the key is that **hips and shoulders stay aligned** in the same type.

steps.title: Protecting young fast bowlers
steps.body:
- Research links a **mixed action** (hips and shoulders pointing in quite different directions at back-foot contact, with lots of counter-rotation) with **lower-back stress fractures** in young fast bowlers.
- **Bowling too much, too soon** is another major risk. Many cricket boards publish overs-per-spell and per-day limits for young fast bowlers — follow your coach's and board's guidance.
- Persistent lower-back pain when bowling is **not** something to bowl through. See a doctor or sports physiotherapist.

steps.title: Line and length
steps.body:
A bowler's first job is **accuracy**. Most wickets come from a consistent **good length** on or just outside **off stump** — the 'corridor of uncertainty', where the batter is unsure whether to play or leave.

Lengths, from the batter's view: **yorker** (at the toes), **full**, **good length**, **short of a length**, **bouncer** (short, rising high).

steps.title: Try this: target bowling
steps.body: Place a cone or a cap on a good length just outside off stump. Bowl 6 balls at it, scoring 2 for a direct hit, 1 for within a bat's length. Track your score every session — accuracy improves faster than you think.

activity.prompt: Bowling session safety & skill checklist
items: Warm up for 10 minutes: jog, dynamic stretches, gradually faster run-throughs

Ask a coach to film your action from behind once a month

quiz.why: Some part of the front foot, grounded or raised, behind the popping crease.

quiz.why: The tolerance is 15 degrees.

quiz.why: Persistent back pain can be a stress injury and needs assessment.
