lessons.title: Pace, seam and swing

story.title: Sam from Durban learns to swing it

scenes.text: Sam, 17, in Durban, South Africa, bowls fast and straight but the ball never moves.
His coach shows him how to hold the seam upright and angled towards the slips.
In the first overs with a new ball, Sam's deliveries start curving away from the right-handers.
He takes three wickets caught behind and grins: 'It's physics, not magic!'

steps.title: The basic seam grip
steps.body:
- Hold the ball with your **index and middle fingers** either side of the seam, close together on top.
- The **thumb** rests underneath on the seam.
- Keep the ball in the **fingers, not the palm** — a gap between ball and palm.
- At release, the wrist is **behind the ball** and the seam is upright.

A ball that lands on an upright seam can **'seam'** — deviate off the pitch.

steps.title: Conventional swing
steps.body:
Swing is movement **in the air**. Bowlers keep one side of the ball shiny by polishing it (with sweat or on clothing — **saliva has been banned in international cricket since 2022**).

For **conventional swing** with a newer ball:
- The ball tends to swing **in the direction the seam points**, towards the rougher side.
- **Outswinger** (moves away from a right-hander): seam angled towards the **slips**, shiny side facing the leg side.
- **Inswinger** (moves into a right-hander): seam angled towards **fine leg**, shiny side facing the off side.

An older, scuffed ball at high pace can **reverse swing** — moving towards the shiny side.

steps.title: Variations
steps.body:
- **Yorker**: a full ball at the toes — great at the end of an innings.
- **Bouncer**: short ball rising towards head height — use sparingly; there are limits on short balls per over in playing conditions.
- **Slower ball**: changes grip (e.g., off-cutter, knuckle ball, back-of-the-hand) to deceive the batter.
- **Cutters**: fingers roll across the seam to make the ball grip and deviate off the pitch.

Master line and length first — variations work only when the stock ball is accurate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Chasing pace by **over-striding** or bowling flat out without control.
- Holding the ball too deep in the palm → no swing, inconsistent pace.
- Using too many variations — batters line up the predictable 'surprise'.
- Bowling at full pace without a proper warm-up.

steps.title: Try this: swing experiment
steps.body: With a partner, bowl 6 balls holding the seam towards slip and 6 towards fine leg. Note which way each moved (or didn't). Swing depends on seam position, release, pace and conditions — keep a notebook of what works.

cards.back: Seam angled towards slips; shiny side on the leg side; moves away from the batter.
Seam angled towards fine leg; shiny side on the off side; moves into the batter.
Older, scuffed ball at high pace moving towards the shiny side.
Deviation off the pitch when the ball lands on an upright seam.
Full ball aimed at the batter's toes.
Fingers roll across the seam so the ball grips and deviates off the pitch.

quiz.q: For conventional swing, the ball tends to move…
options: In the direction the seam points
quiz.why: With conventional swing the ball moves the way the seam points, towards the rough side.

quiz.q: An outswinger to a right-hander has the seam angled towards…
quiz.why: Seam towards slips for the outswinger.

quiz.q: Which is banned for shining the ball in international cricket?
quiz.why: The ICC banned saliva on the ball permanently in 2022.

quiz.q: Reverse swing typically happens with…
options: An older, scuffed ball at high pace
quiz.why: Reverse swing occurs with older balls at pace.

lessons.title: Spin bowling basics: off-spin and leg-spin

scenes.text: Farhan, 11, in Hyderabad, is too small to bowl fast. He's sad at selection time.
His grandfather, a former club spinner, shows him how to flick the ball out of the back of his hand.
The ball dips, lands and spins away. The older boys in the nets are bamboozled.
Farhan is now his team's first-choice spinner. 'Size doesn't matter in spin,' his grandfather says.

steps.title: Off-spin (finger spin)
steps.body:
For a right-arm off-spinner:

- Spread the **index and middle fingers** wide across the seam, top joints on the seam.
- The **index finger** does most of the work; the thumb is lightly on the side or not used.
- At release, turn the wrist and fingers **clockwise** (like turning a door knob), so the ball spins.
- To a right-handed batter, the ball turns **from off to leg** (into the batter).

Left-arm orthodox spinners use the same finger technique and turn the ball **away** from a right-hander.

steps.title: Leg-spin (wrist spin)
steps.body:
For a right-arm leg-spinner:

- First two fingers across the seam on top; the **third (ring) finger bent along the seam** does the spinning; thumb lightly on the side.
- At release, the **wrist flicks** and the third finger rolls the ball out over the top, palm facing the batter/leg side.
- To a right-hander, the stock leg-break turns **from leg to off** (away from the batter).
- The **googly** is a leg-spinner's ball released out of the back of the hand that turns the **other way** — into the right-hander.

steps.title: Flight, drift and dip
steps.body:
Spin is not just turn:

- **Flight**: tossing the ball up on a higher arc to tempt the batter.
- **Drift**: sideways movement in the air before landing, caused by the spin.
- **Dip**: the ball dropping sooner than expected because of over-spin.
- **Pace changes** and **angle changes** (using the crease) are a spinner's best weapons.

A spinner who **spins it hard** and lands it consistently will take wickets at every level.

steps.title: Common spin mistakes
steps.body:
- **Pushing** the ball instead of spinning it — it lands flat and gets hit.
- Bowling too short (easy to pull or cut).
- Fear of being hit → bowling flat and fast. Spinners need courage to flight it.
- Not using the body: a strong pivot and follow-through help both accuracy and spin.

steps.title: Drill: spin to yourself
steps.body: Spin a ball from hand to hand while watching TV — 100 flicks a day builds finger and wrist strength. Then bowl at a single stump from half-length (about 11 yards), aiming to make the ball turn past a shoe placed in line.

activity.prompt: Match the delivery with its description (right-arm bowler, right-hand batter).

Wrist spin turning from leg to off

quiz.why: The index finger imparts off-spin.

quiz.q: A right-arm leg-break to a right-hander turns…
quiz.why: Leg-breaks turn from leg to off, away from a right-hander.

quiz.q: A googly is…
options: A leg-spinner's ball that turns the other way
quiz.why: The googly turns from off to leg, out of the back of the hand.

quiz.q: Which is a common mistake for young spinners?
options: Pushing the ball flat instead of spinning it
quiz.why: Pushing the ball removes the spin and makes it easy to hit.

lessons.title: Fielding: stopping, catching and throwing

story.title: The catch that won the final

scenes.text: Vikram, 13, from Mysuru, can't bat or bowl well enough to be a star. He's put at cover.
He spends every evening with a tennis ball against a wall: 200 catches, left hand, right hand, both.
In the final, the opposition's best batter drives hard and low. Vikram dives and holds it.
'Catches win matches,' his coach says, handing him the man-of-the-match award.

steps.title: Ready position and walking in
steps.body: As the bowler runs in, fielders in the ring **walk in** a few steps so they're moving and on the balls of their feet when the ball is hit. Knees slightly bent, hands ready, eyes on the bat.

steps.title: The long barrier
steps.body:
For a ball coming straight at you on the ground when you can't afford a miss (e.g., in the deep):

- Turn **side-on** to the ball.
- Go down on one knee so the knee touches the heel of the other foot — your leg forms a **barrier** behind your hands.
- Hands together, fingers pointing down, in front of the knee.
- Head over the ball; watch it into the hands.

In the ring, where speed matters, use an **attacking pick-up**: run in, pick up beside the leading foot, and throw in one movement.

steps.title: Catching
steps.body:
- **High catches** (above the chest): fingers pointing **up**, hands near the eyes, thumbs together; or the 'reverse cup' near the chest — follow your coach's method and practise one consistently.
- **Low catches**: fingers pointing **down**, little fingers together.
- Watch the ball all the way; **soft hands** — 'give' with the ball by drawing the hands back.
- Get your body **behind and under** the ball when you can.
- Call **'Mine!'** loudly for skied catches to avoid collisions.

steps.title: Throwing accurately
steps.body:
- Turn **side-on**, point your front shoulder and non-throwing arm at the target.
- Throw **over the top**, stepping towards the target; follow through.
- In the deep, use a **crow hop** (a skip step) to build momentum.
- Aim to reach the keeper or bowler **on the full or one bounce at bail height** over the stumps.
- Warm up your shoulder gradually before throwing hard.

steps.title: Field positions to learn
steps.body: For a right-hander, off side: **slip, gully, point, cover, extra cover, mid-off, third man, long-off**. Leg side: **fine leg, square leg, mid-wicket, mid-on, long-on, deep mid-wicket, short leg, leg slip**. Behind the bat: the **wicket-keeper**. Close positions like **silly point** and **short leg** need a helmet.

Shoulder stretch and cool-down

options: Touch the heel of the other foot to form a barrier
quiz.why: Knee to heel closes the gap behind the hands.

quiz.q: For a low catch, fingers should point…
quiz.why: Fingers down with little fingers together for low catches.

quiz.q: What do 'soft hands' mean?
options: Giving with the ball as it arrives
quiz.why: Drawing the hands back absorbs the ball and stops it bouncing out.

quiz.q: Why do ring fielders walk in as the bowler runs up?
options: To be moving and ready when the ball is hit
quiz.why: Moving on the balls of the feet improves reaction.

quiz.q: Which close position needs a helmet?
quiz.why: Close catchers like short leg and silly point must protect their heads.

lessons.title: Wicket-keeping basics

scenes.text: Tanvi, 12, in Nagpur, volunteers to keep when her team has nobody else.
In her first match she drops two catches by snatching at the ball.
An older keeper teaches her: 'Stay low, rise with the ball, let it come into the gloves.'
By the end of the season she has 12 dismissals, including two stumpings off the leg-spinner.

steps.title: The stance
steps.body:
- **Squat** with feet about shoulder-width apart, weight on the **balls of the feet**.
- Gloves together in front, **fingers pointing down or sideways — never straight at the ball** (to avoid finger injuries).
- Head still, eyes level, with a clear view of the ball (usually just outside off stump for a right-hander).
- Stay low until the ball pitches, then **rise with the bounce**.

steps.title: Standing back vs standing up
steps.body:
- **Fast and medium bowlers**: stand **back**, far enough that the ball reaches you around waist height after bouncing — distance depends on pace and bounce.
- **Spinners and slower bowlers**: stand **up** to the stumps (close behind them) — this stops batters leaving their crease and creates **stumping** chances.
- When standing up, a **helmet** is strongly recommended.

steps.title: Taking the ball
steps.body:
- Move **feet first** — step across with the outside leg for balls wide of off stump, so the body stays behind the ball.
- Watch the ball **into the gloves**; let the hands 'give' back towards the body.
- For a stumping, take the ball and bring the gloves **straight to the stumps** in one smooth move — don't swing wide.
- Keep the gloves together when possible, opening them like a bowl.

steps.title: Common keeping mistakes and injuries
steps.body:
- **Snatching** at the ball → drops and bruised hands.
- **Fingers pointing at the ball** → broken or dislocated fingers.
- **Standing up too soon** → you can't see the ball.
- Keepers squat hundreds of times a day — strengthen your legs and hips and warm up the knees and hips before play.

steps.title: Drill: wall keeping
steps.body: Stand 3–4 m from a wall in your stance. A partner behind you throws a tennis ball at the wall; you rise and take it. Progress to taking balls wide on both sides, using footwork. 3 sets of 20.

items.back: Down or sideways — never directly at the ball.

items.front: When do you rise from the squat?
items.back: With the bounce of the ball, after it pitches.

items.front: Stand up or back to a spinner?
items.back: Up to the stumps — it creates stumping chances.

items.front: How to take a wide ball outside off?
items.back: Step across with the outside leg; keep the body behind the ball.
Wear a helmet with a grille.

quiz.q: When should a keeper rise from the squat?
options: With the bounce of the ball
quiz.why: Rising with the bounce keeps eyes level with the ball.

quiz.q: Which bowlers does the keeper usually stand up to?
quiz.why: Standing up to spinners creates stumpings.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't fingers point at the ball?
quiz.why: A ball hitting fingertips can break or dislocate them.

options: Watching the ball into the gloves
quiz.why: Snatching leads to the ball bouncing out.

options: Must land within and not touching the return crease
questions.why: The back foot must be inside and not touching the return crease.

questions.q: Where should a keeper stand to a spinner?

courses.summary: How cricketers train their bodies, stay safe in heat, build a strong mind, and how the pathway from school and club cricket to district, state and beyond generally works in India — plus how to avoid fake 'selection' scams.

lessons.title: Fitness for cricketers

scenes.text: Kiran, 16, from Ranchi, is a talented batter but tires badly after 30 overs in the field.
At the state camp, the trainer explains that fitness tests are now part of selection at many levels.
Kiran follows a simple plan: sprints, agility, strength twice a week and proper sleep.
Three months later he's running quicker twos and his last 10 overs are as sharp as his first 10.

steps.title: Before you begin
steps.body: This is general education, not medical advice. **Consult a doctor before starting if you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, diabetes, asthma, a joint or back problem, or are recovering from injury.** Young players should train under a qualified coach. Stop if you feel chest pain, faintness or sharp pain; in an emergency call **112**.

steps.title: What cricket demands
steps.body:
Cricket is a game of **repeated short bursts**: sprinting between wickets, chasing to the boundary, bowling spells, diving, throwing — with recovery in between, often for hours in the heat.

So cricketers need:
- **Speed and acceleration** (first 5–10 m).
- **Agility** (turning, changing direction).
- **Repeated-sprint endurance**.
- **Strength and power** in legs, hips, core and upper body.
- **Shoulder and core robustness** to stay injury-free.
- **Flexibility and mobility** in hips, hamstrings and thoracic spine.

Some teams use the **Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test** to measure repeated running fitness.

steps.title: A sample week for a 15–17-year-old (in season)
steps.body:
- **Mon**: Nets + 6×20 m sprints (full recovery) + core (plank, side plank, dead bug).
- **Tue**: Strength (squat, lunge, push-up, row, hip hinge — technique first) 30–40 min.
- **Wed**: Nets + agility (cone drills, 'turn and run' between wickets).
- **Thu**: Rest or light mobility/yoga.
- **Fri**: Strength + shoulder care (band rotations, wall slides).
- **Sat/Sun**: Matches; light recovery jog and stretch after.

Adjust to your coach's plan. Younger players (under 14) should focus on fun movement skills, bodyweight exercises and lots of different sports.

steps.title: Recovery is training too
steps.body:
- **Sleep**: teenagers generally need 8–10 hours a night.
- **Eat** regular meals with carbohydrate, protein and vegetables; a snack after training.
- **Hydrate** before, during and after (next lesson covers heat).
- **Monitor workload**: sudden jumps in bowling or training load raise injury risk. Increase gradually.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Copying a professional's gym routine at 13.
- Lifting heavy with poor form to 'get big'.
- Skipping warm-ups before nets.
- Taking supplements without advice — some contain banned substances (see the nutrition course).

activity.prompt: Cricket fitness circuit (bodyweight, 25 minutes). Warm up first.
items: Warm-up: 5 min jog + leg swings, hip circles, arm circles
6 × 20 m sprints, walk back recovery
3 × 'run a three' between two cones 20 m apart (practise turns low and fast)
3 × 10 bodyweight squats with good form
3 × 8 lunges each leg
3 × 30-second plank and 20-second side plank each side
2 × 10 band or towel shoulder rotations
Cool-down: walk 3 min, stretch hamstrings, hips, shoulders

quiz.q: Cricket mostly involves…
quiz.why: Sprints, throws and bowling with recovery between.

quiz.q: A key cause of injury in young bowlers is…
quiz.why: Spikes in workload raise injury risk.

quiz.q: How much sleep do teenagers generally need?
quiz.why: Most teens need 8–10 hours.

quiz.q: What should under-14 players focus on?
options: Fun movement skills, bodyweight work and many sports
quiz.why: Broad athletic development comes first.

lessons.title: Playing in the heat: hydration and heat illness

scenes.text: It's 41°C at an under-16 match in Nagpur in April. Rahul has been fielding for three hours.
He feels dizzy, has a headache and stops sweating. He becomes confused about the score.
His coach recognises danger: they move him to shade, cool him with water and ice, and call 112.
Doctors say fast cooling made a big difference. The academy now plans drinks breaks and shade for every match.

steps.title: Why the heat matters
steps.body: In hot, humid weather your body cools itself by sweating. You can lose a lot of fluid and salt in a long session. Even modest dehydration can reduce concentration, decision-making and skill — and severe heat can be dangerous.

steps.title: A simple hydration plan
steps.body:
- **Before**: drink regularly through the day; arrive hydrated (pale-yellow urine is a rough guide).
- **During**: sip at every drinks break and between overs when possible — don't wait to be very thirsty.
- **After**: rehydrate with water and food; in long, sweaty sessions an **ORS** or a drink with some salt helps replace losses.
- Wear a **hat, sunscreen and light, breathable clothing**; rest in the shade.
- Don't force huge amounts of plain water — over-drinking can also be harmful.

steps.title: Know the warning signs
steps.body:
**Heat exhaustion**: heavy sweating, tiredness, headache, dizziness, nausea, cramps. → Stop, move to shade, cool down, sip fluids. If not improving within about 30 minutes, get medical help.

**Heat stroke** (an emergency): very high body temperature, **confusion, strange behaviour, collapse, fits**, skin may be hot (sweating may or may not have stopped). → **Call 112**, move to shade, **cool rapidly** (cold water, ice packs to neck/armpits/groin, fanning) while waiting. Don't give drinks if they can't swallow safely.

steps.title: Smart habits for Indian summers
steps.body:
- Schedule hard training early morning or late afternoon.
- Acclimatise over 1–2 weeks when the heat rises: shorter sessions first.
- Buddy system: team-mates watch each other for warning signs.
- Weigh yourself before and after a long session: each kg lost is roughly a litre of fluid to replace gradually.

a.text: You're captain in a 40°C match. Your fielder at fine leg looks unsteady and says he has a headache. What do you do first?

choices.label: Tell him to keep going till the drinks break
choices.feedback: Waiting can let things get worse quickly.

choices.label: Stop play, bring him off into the shade and tell the coach
choices.feedback: Right — act early.

b.text: Two overs later he collapses and seems confused. Now what?

choices.label: Call 112, move him to shade, cool him rapidly with water and ice
choices.feedback: Correct emergency response for suspected heat stroke.

c.text: In the shade he is sweating a lot but can talk clearly. What next?

choices.label: Cool him, give sips of water/ORS, rest, and monitor; get medical help if not better in about 30 min or he gets confused
choices.feedback: Good management of likely heat exhaustion.

choices.label: Give him an energy drink and send him back out
choices.feedback: Sending him back too soon is risky.

end1.text: He recovers. You arrange extra drinks breaks for everyone. Great leadership.

end2.text: Rapid cooling and calling 112 are exactly right. Next time, act at the first warning sign.

quiz.q: Confusion and collapse in the heat suggest…

lessons.title: The mental game: routines, focus and bouncing back

scenes.text: Zara, 15, a Mumbai opener, gets out first ball in an important match and cries in the dressing room.
Her coach doesn't talk about technique. She asks, 'What were you thinking before that ball?' 'That I mustn't fail,' says Zara.
They build a simple routine for every ball: breathe, look at the bat, a trigger word — 'Watch' — then focus.
Next match she scores 47. 'I didn't think about the score at all. Just one ball at a time.'

steps.title: Between-ball routines
steps.body:
A cricket ball takes under a second to reach you, but there are ~30 seconds between balls. What you do with that time matters.

A simple batting routine:
1. **Switch off**: walk towards square leg, relax your grip, look at something neutral.
2. **Review quickly**: 'Was that good? Fine. Next.'
3. **Breathe**: one slow breath out.
4. **Switch on**: take stance, a trigger word ('Watch', 'Ball'), eyes on the bowler's hand.

Bowlers can do the same at the top of their run-up: plan the ball, picture it, breathe, go.

steps.title: Process goals beat outcome goals
steps.body:
- **Outcome goal**: 'Score 50', 'Take 3 wickets' — you don't fully control these.
- **Process goal**: 'Watch the ball out of the hand', 'Leave well outside off', 'Hit the top of off stump' — you control these.

Focus on processes during play; the outcomes follow more often.

steps.title: Self-talk and handling failure
steps.body:
- Replace 'Don't get out' (which puts 'getting out' in your head) with **'Watch the ball'**.
- After a mistake, use a **reset**: a breath, a word, a physical action (adjusting gloves).
- Remember cricket's maths: even great batters fail often. Judge yourself over a season, not one innings.
- Keep a **cricket diary**: one thing that went well, one thing to work on, after each game.

steps.title: When to talk to someone
steps.body: Pressure from selection, parents or social media can feel heavy. If worry affects your sleep, eating or enjoyment for weeks, talk to a trusted adult or coach. In India, **Tele-MANAS (14416)** offers free mental-health support.

activity.label: Pre-ball reset: breathe in 4, hold 2, out 6. Use it before every ball in the nets this week.

quiz.q: Why say 'Watch the ball' rather than 'Don't get out'?

quiz.q: What is the purpose of 'switching off' between balls?
options: To rest the mind so you can fully focus for the next ball
quiz.why: Nobody can concentrate intensely for hours; routines help you switch on when it counts.

quiz.why: Tele-MANAS is 14416; 1098 is Childline.

lessons.title: The pathway in India: school, club, district, state and beyond

story.title: Pooja's road from a small town

scenes.text: Pooja, 13, from a small town in Haryana, plays with boys in the local maidan and wants to play for India.
Her PE teacher enters her school in inter-school matches and tells her about the district association's women's trials.
Her father collects her birth certificate and school records for age verification, and they register properly.
A man offers a 'guaranteed state selection' for ₹1.5 lakh. Her coach says: real selection is never sold. They walk away.
Two seasons of hard work later, Pooja is picked for her state's under-age squad.

steps.title: The general ladder
steps.body:
Details differ by state and change over time, but generally in India:

1. **School and local cricket**: inter-school tournaments, school games (including the School Games Federation of India events), local leagues.
2. **Clubs and academies**: regular coaching and matches in leagues run or recognised by the local/district association.
3. **District association**: holds **trials and age-group selections** (e.g., under-14, under-16, under-19) and inter-district tournaments.
4. **State association** (affiliated to the **BCCI**): picks state age-group and senior teams for national domestic tournaments.
5. **Zonal / national camps, India A and India teams** — for the very best performers.

Women's cricket has its own age-group and senior domestic tournaments, and professional leagues like the WPL.

steps.title: Some BCCI domestic tournaments
steps.body:
- **Ranji Trophy**: senior men's multi-day (first-class).
- **Vijay Hazare Trophy**: senior men's one-day.
- **Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy**: senior men's T20.
- **Cooch Behar Trophy** (U-19 multi-day) and **Vinoo Mankad Trophy** (U-19 one-day).
- **Vijay Merchant Trophy**: U-16.

Tournament formats and age limits can change; always check your state association's current notices.

steps.title: Practical steps
steps.body:
- **Register** with a club or academy affiliated to your district association.
- Keep **age documents** ready (birth certificate, school records). Age-group cricket requires age verification; age fraud can bring long bans.
- Watch for **trial notices** on official association websites and notice boards.
- Build a **record**: scorecards from recognised matches matter more than videos.
- Keep up your **studies** — very few players become professionals, and many coaches, physios, analysts, umpires and scorers also work in cricket. Coaching qualifications (e.g., NIS or board coaching courses) open careers too.

steps.title: Red flags: selection scams
steps.body:
- Anyone promising **guaranteed selection** for a state team or an IPL/WPL franchise for money.
- 'Trials' with high fees and no link to an official association.
- Pressure to pay quickly in cash, or to hide things from parents.
- Requests to change or 'adjust' age documents.

Genuine selection is based on performance in recognised cricket. If something feels wrong, check directly with the district or state association, and talk to your parents and coach.

b.text: After paying, the number stops answering. What now?

choices.feedback: Reporting quickly helps and may stop others being cheated.

c.text: Your coach finds no such trial on any official website. Your next step?

choices.label: Ignore it and focus on the district association's real trials
choices.feedback: Exactly — performance in recognised cricket is the real route.

choices.label: Pay anyway, just in case
choices.feedback: 'Just in case' is how scams win.

end1.text: You train hard, register with your district, and get noticed in recognised matches. That's the real pathway.

end2.text: A painful lesson, but reporting is right. Real trials never sell guaranteed places.

lessons.title: The court, scoring and serving rules

scenes.text: Aisha, 12, from Hyderabad, plays badminton every evening in her colony — with no lines and her own rules.
At her first district tournament, the umpire calls 'Service fault!' twice. She doesn't know why.
Her coach shows her the service height rule and which court to serve from.
She wins her next match 21–17, 21–15 — with zero service faults.

steps.title: The court
steps.body:
- Court length **13.4 m**; width **6.1 m** for doubles and **5.18 m** for singles.
- The net is **1.524 m (5 ft) high at the centre** and 1.55 m at the posts.
- **Singles**: long and narrow — use the inner side lines and the back boundary line.
- **Doubles**: wide — outer side lines; for the **serve**, the **doubles long service line** (0.76 m inside the back line) is the back limit, so the doubles service box is wide but short.

steps.title: Rally-point scoring
steps.body:
- Every rally wins a point, whoever served.
- A game is won by the first to **21 points**, but you must lead by **2**. At **29–29**, the next point wins (so 30 is the maximum).
- A match is **best of three games**.
- There is a short interval when the leading side reaches **11**, and a break between games.
- The side that wins a rally serves next.

steps.title: Service rules
steps.body:
- Server and receiver stand in **diagonally opposite service courts**, feet in contact with the floor and **not touching the lines**, until the serve is made.
- In singles, serve from the **right** service court when your score is **even** (0, 2, 4…) and from the **left** when it's **odd**.
- The whole shuttle must be **below 1.15 m from the court surface** when hit (current BWF rule), and you hit the **base (cork) of the shuttle first**.
- One continuous forward swing — no feints or delays once the serve starts.
- The serve must land in the receiver's diagonal service court; landing on the line is **in**.

steps.title: Common faults
steps.body:
- Serving with the shuttle **too high**.
- Stepping on a line or moving the feet before the serve.
- A **double hit** or carrying the shuttle (slinging it).
- Touching the net with the racket or body during play.
- Shuttle hitting your body — it's your fault.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Play a practice game with a friend where you **say the score aloud before every serve**, server's score first. Check you're serving from the right court for even, left for odd.

lessons.title: Grips and the ready position

scenes.text: Wei, 10, in Singapore, holds his racket like a frying pan, face flat towards the net.
His backhand never reaches the back of the court.
His coach shows him the 'handshake' forehand grip and the thumb-up backhand grip.
Within a month his clears reach the back line from both sides.

steps.title: Forehand grip (the handshake)
steps.body:
- Hold the racket with the **frame edge facing you** (racket face perpendicular to the floor).
- 'Shake hands' with the handle: a **V** between thumb and index finger sits on the top-left bevel (for right-handers).
- Fingers slightly spread; index finger a little apart like a trigger.
- Hold **loosely** — tighten only at the moment of hitting for power.

steps.title: Backhand grip (thumb grip)
steps.body:
- From the forehand grip, turn the racket slightly so the **thumb pad sits flat on the wide back bevel** of the handle.
- The thumb pushes through the shuttle on backhand shots.
- Switch between forehand and backhand grips quickly using your fingers — practise this a lot.

steps.title: Ready position and the split step
steps.body:
- Stand near the **centre (base)** of your court, feet shoulder-width, knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet.
- Racket **up** in front of you.
- As the opponent hits, do a small **split step** (a little hop landing on both feet) so you can push off instantly in any direction.

steps.title: Common grip mistakes
steps.body:
- **Frying-pan grip**: no power on backhands and stiff wrist.
- **Squeezing too hard**: tires the forearm and reduces speed and touch; can contribute to elbow pain.
- Holding the racket too close to the head of the handle — hold it lower for reach and power (shorter for net play).

steps.title: Grip switch drill
steps.body: With a racket in hand, switch from forehand to backhand grip and back 20 times without looking, using only your fingers. Then shadow 10 forehand and 10 backhand swings, relaxing the grip between each.

lessons.title: Footwork: moving to all six corners

scenes.text: Priyanka, 15, from Lucknow, can hit every shot — if she arrives in time. Mostly she doesn't.
Her coach marks six spots on the court and makes her 'shadow' to each and back to base.
She learns the chassé, the crossover, and the lunge with her racket leg forward.
Two months later she's reaching shots she'd have given up on.

steps.title: Six corners and the base
steps.body: Think of the court as **six target areas**: two at the net, two at the mid-court sides, two at the back. After every shot, **recover to the base** (roughly the centre of your court, slightly behind the middle in singles).

steps.title: Key steps
steps.body:
- **Split step** as the opponent hits.
- **Chassé**: a side-step where one foot chases the other without crossing — quick and balanced.
- **Crossover step** for longer distances.
- **Lunge** at the net and sides: step with the **racket-side leg forward** (right leg for right-handers), heel landing first, knee over the ankle (not beyond the toes), back leg extended for balance.
- **Recover**: push back from the lunge to the base.

steps.title: Moving to the back
steps.body: For a high shuttle to your forehand rear corner: turn sideways, use chassé steps back, get **behind the shuttle**, then hit with a scissor-kick (legs switch in the air) or a jump if appropriate, landing balanced. For the backhand rear corner, many players use a **round-the-head** forehand when possible because it's stronger than a backhand.

steps.title: Protect your knees and ankles
steps.body:
- Never let the knee collapse inward or go far beyond the toes when lunging.
- Wear **non-marking court shoes** with grip and cushioning — not running shoes.
- Warm up the ankles, knees and hips before playing.

General education, not medical advice. Persistent knee or ankle pain → see a doctor or physio.

lessons.title: The strokes: clear, drop, smash, net shot and serve

scenes.text: Anjali and Joel, 14, from Kochi, play doubles but only know one shot: hit hard.
Their coach teaches them: clear to push back, drop to bring forward, smash to finish, net shot to force a lift.

steps.title: Overhead clear
steps.body:
- Turn **side-on**, non-racket arm up pointing at the shuttle, racket back.
- Hit the shuttle **high and in front** of you at full stretch.
- Rotate the trunk, forearm rotation (pronation) through contact; snap at impact.
- **Defensive clear**: high and deep to the back line, buying time. **Attacking clear**: flatter and faster over the opponent.

steps.title: Drop shot and smash
steps.body:
- **Drop**: same preparation as a clear (disguise!), but slow the racket at contact and guide the shuttle steeply just over the net.
- **Smash**: same preparation; hit the shuttle **in front** of the body, steeply downward, with full body rotation and forearm pronation. Use it when the shuttle is high and you're well-balanced, not from deep behind your body.
- Aim smashes at the opponent's body, the side lines, or the gap between doubles players.

steps.title: Net shot and lift
steps.body:
- **Net shot**: lunge in, racket up, gently **tumble or push** the shuttle just over the net so it falls close to the tape on the other side.
- **Lift**: from the net, push the shuttle high and deep to the back of the opponent's court when you can't play a net shot.
- Take the shuttle **as high as possible** at the net — the higher you meet it, the more options you have.

steps.title: The low serve
steps.body:
- Common in doubles and increasingly in singles: a short, flat serve that just clears the net and lands near the **short service line**.
- Backhand low serve: racket in front, short push with the thumb, shuttle below 1.15 m.
- The **high serve** (forehand, deep to the back line) is used in singles to push the opponent back.

steps.title: Common stroke mistakes
steps.body:
- Hitting overheads **behind the head** → weak shots and shoulder strain.
- Telegraphing the drop (obvious slow swing) → opponent reads it.
- Smashing every shuttle — you'll tire and become predictable.
- Not recovering to base after the shot.

lessons.title: Tennis scoring and rules

scenes.text: Mrs. Kapoor, 62, from Delhi, takes up tennis after retiring. 'Why is zero called love?' she laughs.
Her coach, Neil, explains: 15, 30, 40, game — and that the history of the names is debated.
She keeps score aloud every point until it becomes automatic.
Six months later she wins her first club doubles match 6–4, 7–6.

steps.title: Points and games
steps.body:
Points in a game go: **0 (love) → 15 → 30 → 40 → game**.

- At **40–40** it's **deuce**. The next point gives **advantage**; win it again to win the game. Lose it and it's back to deuce.
- The **server's score is said first**: '30–15' means the server has 30.
- Some formats use **no-ad** scoring: at deuce, the next point wins.

steps.title: Sets and tie-breaks
steps.body:
- A **set** is won by the first to **6 games** with a lead of **2** (6–4, 7–5).
- At **6–6**, most sets use a **tie-break**: first to **7 points** with a 2-point lead. In tie-breaks, points are counted normally (1, 2, 3…).
- Since 2022, all four Grand Slam tournaments play a **10-point tie-break** at 6–6 in the deciding set.
- Matches are best of 3 sets (or best of 5 in men's Grand Slam singles).

steps.title: Serving and play
steps.body:
- The server stands **behind the baseline**, between the centre mark and the side line, and serves **diagonally** into the opposite service box. The first point of each game is served from the **right (deuce) side**, then alternate.
- Two attempts: miss both = **double fault** (point lost).
- A serve that clips the net and lands in is a **let** — replayed.
- **Foot fault**: touching the baseline or court with a foot before hitting the ball.
- In a rally, the ball may bounce **once** (or be volleyed before it bounces). A ball touching any part of the line is **in**.
- Players change ends after the 1st, 3rd, 5th… game of each set.

steps.title: Etiquette
steps.body:
- Call the score clearly before serving.
- In matches without umpires, you call lines on **your side** — and if unsure, the ball is **in** for your opponent.
- Don't walk behind a court while a point is being played.

lessons.title: Tennis grips, groundstrokes, volley and serve

scenes.text: Kavya, 13, in Pune, hits her forehand with a flat wrist and a very late swing.
Her coach films it: no unit turn, no follow-through.
They practise 'turn, drop, swing, finish over the shoulder' with a semi-western grip.
Her forehand becomes her weapon — heavy topspin landing deep.

steps.title: The main grips
steps.body:
Picture the handle as an octagon with 8 bevels. The base knuckle of your index finger sits on a different bevel for each grip.

- **Continental** ('hammer grip'): used for **serves, volleys, overheads and slices**.
- **Eastern forehand** ('shake hands with the racket'): good for flatter forehands.
- **Semi-western**: hand turned further under the handle — good for **topspin** forehands; very common today.
- **Backhand**: one-handed (eastern backhand) or two-handed (dominant hand continental, other hand eastern forehand above it).

steps.title: Groundstrokes: forehand and backhand
steps.body:
1. **Ready position**, split step as the opponent hits.
2. **Unit turn**: turn shoulders and hips early, racket back.
3. **Move** to the ball and set your feet.
4. **Swing low to high** for topspin, contacting the ball **in front** of the body around waist height.
5. **Follow through** — over the shoulder for a forehand.
6. **Recover** to the centre of the baseline.

steps.title: Volley
steps.body:
- Continental grip, racket up in front.
- **Short punch**, no big backswing; step forward into the ball.
- Firm wrist; contact in front of the body.

steps.title: The serve
steps.body:
- Continental grip; side-on stance behind the baseline.
- **Toss** slightly in front and towards your hitting side, high enough to hit at full stretch. A consistent toss is the foundation of a consistent serve.
- **Trophy position**: tossing arm up, racket back, knees bent.
- Drive up through the ball, pronating the forearm, and follow through across the body.
- Beginners can start with a simpler 'abbreviated' motion and add rhythm later.

steps.title: Avoiding tennis elbow and shoulder strain
steps.body:
- Squeezing the grip too hard and late, arm-only swings, and a heavy or badly strung racket can contribute to **lateral elbow pain** ('tennis elbow').
- Use the **legs and trunk**, not just the arm. Warm up the shoulder.
- Persistent pain → rest and see a doctor or physiotherapist. General education, not medical advice.

lessons.title: Table tennis: rules and the legal serve

scenes.text: Ritika, 11, plays table tennis at her community centre in Chennai, hiding the ball behind her hand on serves.
At a local tournament, the umpire calls her serve illegal.
Her coach teaches her the service law: open palm, toss at least 16 cm, ball visible.
Her new legal serve is just as tricky — and she reaches the semi-final.

steps.title: The table and ball
steps.body:
- Table: **2.74 m long, 1.525 m wide, 76 cm high**.
- Net: **15.25 cm** high.
- Ball: **40 mm** diameter (plastic in modern competitions).
- Racket: the two sides must have different colours — one **black**, the other a bright contrasting colour (traditionally red).

steps.title: Scoring
steps.body:
- A game is won by the first to **11 points** with a **2-point lead**.
- Matches are best of an odd number of games (e.g., best of 5 or 7).
- **Service changes every 2 points**. At **10–10**, each player serves **one point** in turn until someone leads by 2.
- Players change ends after each game, and in the last possible game when someone reaches 5 points.

steps.title: The legal serve
steps.body:
- The ball starts resting on your **open, flat, stationary palm**.
- Toss it **near-vertically upwards at least 16 cm**, without spin, and hit it as it **falls**.
- From the start of the serve until it's struck, the ball must be **above the level of the playing surface** and **behind your end line**.
- The ball must **not be hidden** from the receiver by your body or arm.
- It must bounce **once on your side**, then **once on the receiver's side**.
- In singles, you can serve anywhere on the receiver's side. In **doubles**, serve **diagonally from your right half to the receiver's right half**.
- If the serve touches the net and is otherwise good, it's a **let** — replayed.

steps.title: Common faults
steps.body:
- Tossing from cupped fingers or throwing the ball sideways.
- Hiding the contact with your free arm or body.
- Volleying the ball before it bounces on your side (in a rally that's a lost point).
- Touching the table with your free hand, or moving the table, during a rally.

lessons.title: Table tennis grips, strokes and spin

scenes.text: Mr. Sharma, 70, from Indore, has played table tennis every morning for 40 years.
His grandson Dev, 12, hits hard but every return from grandpa comes back with heavy backspin into the net.
Grandpa explains: 'Read the spin. Open your bat to lift backspin. Brush up for topspin.'
A month later Dev loops grandpa's chop for a winner. They both cheer.

steps.title: Grips
steps.body:
- **Shakehand**: like shaking hands — thumb and index finger on either side of the blade, other fingers around the handle. Balanced for forehand and backhand; most common.
- **Penhold**: held like a pen, popular in parts of Asia; strong forehand and wrist play, backhand techniques vary.
- Keep the grip **relaxed**; the **neutral** grip (no strong forehand or backhand bias) is best for beginners.

steps.title: Understanding spin
steps.body:
- **Topspin**: bat brushes **up** the back of the ball; the ball dips down and kicks forward after the bounce. To return it, **close** the bat face (angle it forward).
- **Backspin (underspin)**: bat brushes **under** the ball; the ball floats and checks. To return it, **open** the bat face (angle it back) and lift.
- **Sidespin**: bat brushes the side; the ball curves and kicks sideways.

Watch the **opponent's bat movement** to read spin.

steps.title: The four basic strokes
steps.body:
- **Forehand drive (counter-hit)**: small backswing, rotate waist, bat closed, brush slightly forward-upward, finish near the forehead.
- **Backhand drive**: bat in front of the body, elbow forward, flick forward from the elbow and forearm.
- **Push**: a short, controlled backspin stroke against backspin — open bat, push forward and under.
- **Block**: against fast topspin attacks — short stroke, bat angle closed, use the opponent's pace.

Then the **loop** (heavy topspin attack) builds on the drive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swinging with the arm only — use the **waist and legs**.
- Standing too close or too far from the table (about an arm's length plus a bit is a common starting point).
- Not watching the opponent's bat → misreading spin.
- Big backswings — table tennis rewards compact strokes.

steps.title: Drill: rally counter
steps.body: With a partner, rally forehand-to-forehand diagonally. Count your longest rally. Then backhand-to-backhand. Then one player pushes, the other pushes back. Aim for 50-ball rallies.

quiz.why: Shakehand is most common.

quiz.why: Bat path reveals the spin.

lessons.title: Sprinting: starts, mechanics and relays

scenes.text: Sunita, 14, the fastest girl in her school in Patiala, flinches before the gun at the district meet.
She's disqualified — one false start and you're out.
Her coach teaches her to focus on the sound, not to guess, and to practise 'set' holds.
At the next meet she waits for the gun, explodes out, and wins the 100 m.

steps.title: The crouch start
steps.body:
- **'On your marks'**: feet in the blocks (front foot about 1.5–2 foot-lengths behind the line, back foot further back), knee of the back leg on the ground, hands just behind the line, shoulder-width apart, fingers bridged, arms straight.
- **'Set'**: raise the hips slightly above the shoulders, shoulders over or slightly ahead of the hands, weight forward, still.
- **Gun**: drive powerfully from both legs, the back leg swinging through first; arms pump hard; stay low for the first several strides, rising gradually.

steps.title: False starts
steps.body: Under World Athletics rules, **one false start leads to disqualification** in most events. Starting blocks with sensors treat a reaction faster than **0.100 seconds** after the gun as a false start, because humans can't genuinely react that fast. Moving after 'Set' but before the gun also counts.

steps.title: Sprint mechanics
steps.body:
- Run **tall** at top speed, slight forward lean from the ankles.
- Land on the **balls of the feet**, under the hips, not far in front.
- **High knee drive**, heel coming up under the hip.
- **Arms** swing forward and back (not across the body), elbows about 90°, hands relaxed (cheek to hip).
- **Relax** the face and shoulders — tension slows you down.

steps.title: Relay baton exchange (4×100 m)
steps.body:
- The baton must be passed **within the marked changeover zone** (30 m in current rules for the 4×100); where the baton is, not the runners, decides.
- The incoming runner shouts a signal ('Hand!'); the outgoing runner, already accelerating from a check mark, puts a hand back.
- **Upsweep** (hand low, baton pushed up) or **downsweep** (hand high, baton pushed down into a palm-up hand).
- Runners usually alternate hands so they stay on the inside or outside of the lane appropriately.
- Practise again and again — exchanges win or lose relays.

steps.title: Try this: drills
steps.body: A-skips (high knee skipping), B-skips, high knees, butt kicks, 3 × 20 m from a crouch start, and 4 × 30 m flying sprints (jog in 20 m, sprint 30 m). Walk back for full recovery — sprint training is about **quality**, not exhaustion.

lessons.title: Middle and long distance: pacing and training

scenes.text: Kiprono, 16, runs at a school in Eldoret, Kenya. He loves to sprint the first lap of the 1500 m — and fade badly.
His coach gives him a stopwatch and target lap times.
He learns to run even laps and save something for the last 300 m.
He wins the county final, passing three runners on the last bend.

steps.title: Pacing
steps.body:
- **Even pace**: similar lap times throughout — efficient for most runners.
- **Negative split**: second half slightly faster than the first — a strong strategy for longer races.
- Starting too fast builds fatigue early and you slow down a lot.

On a standard **400 m track**, a 1600 m run is **4 laps**; the 1500 m is 3¾ laps.

steps.title: Worked example: lap targets
steps.body: Goal: 1600 m in 8 minutes (480 seconds). That's 4 laps → **120 seconds (2:00) per lap**, or 60 seconds per 200 m. Check at every lap; if you're at 1:50, ease off slightly; if 2:10, gradually pick it up.

steps.title: Building endurance safely
steps.body:
- **Easy runs** (most of your running): at a pace where you can talk in sentences.
- **Intervals**: e.g., 6 × 400 m at goal race pace with 90 s rest.
- **Tempo runs**: 15–20 min at 'comfortably hard'.
- **Increase weekly distance gradually**; a common rule of thumb is no more than about 10% a week.
- Rest days and sleep let the body adapt.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Consult a doctor before starting if you have heart, lung or other conditions. Stop and get help for chest pain, fainting or unusual breathlessness. Avoid hard running in extreme heat; hydrate. Pain that changes how you run (limping) → stop and get it checked. Emergency: **112**.

quiz.why: Gradual increases reduce injury risk.

lessons.title: Jumping: long jump and high jump basics

scenes.text: Neel, 13, from Thiruvananthapuram, jumps far — but his first three attempts are all no-jumps.
His coach measures his run-up from the board backwards and marks a check point.
He practises hitting the board without looking down.
In the final, his first legal jump wins the bronze medal.

steps.title: Long jump phases
steps.body:
1. **Approach**: a consistent, accelerating run-up (beginners often use 8–12 strides; experienced jumpers longer). Measure it from the board and mark it.
2. **Take-off**: from **one foot** on the board, driving the opposite knee and arms upward; head up, eyes forward.
3. **Flight**: hold a balanced position (sail, hang or hitch-kick techniques).
4. **Landing**: extend legs forward, then fall forward or sideways — **not back**.

steps.title: Long jump rules
steps.body:
- It's a **foul (no-jump)** if any part of the take-off foot goes **beyond the take-off line** (the front edge of the board).
- The jump is measured from the **take-off line** to the **nearest mark in the sand** made by any part of the body.
- So falling backwards after landing loses distance.

steps.title: High jump basics
steps.body:
- Take-off from **one foot** (two-foot take-offs are not allowed).
- Modern technique is the **Fosbury flop**: a **curved (J-shaped) approach**, take-off from the foot further from the bar, rotate to go over **back-first**, and land on the shoulders/upper back on a **proper landing mat**.
- Beginners can learn the **scissors** technique first.
- Three consecutive failures at a height eliminate you.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body:
- **Never attempt the flop without a proper high-jump landing mat.**
- Dig and rake the long jump pit before jumping; check it for stones or glass.
- Warm up thoroughly; jumps stress the ankles, knees and hamstrings.

statements.why: Any part of the take-off foot beyond the line = no-jump.

statements.why: To the nearest mark made by any part of the body.

statements.s: You may practise the Fosbury flop onto grass if you're careful.
statements.why: Always use a proper landing mat.

statements.s: Falling backwards after landing can cost distance in long jump.
statements.why: The mark nearest the board is measured.

quiz.why: The nearest mark to the take-off line.

quiz.q: High jump take-off must be from…
quiz.why: One-foot take-off is required.

quiz.why: A curved run-up helps rotation.

quiz.q: How many consecutive failures eliminate a high jumper?

lessons.title: Throwing: shot put technique and throwing safety

scenes.text: At a school sports day in Bhopal, a student walks across the throwing area to fetch a lost bottle.
Coach Rekha blows her whistle — a shot has just landed two metres away from him.
She stops the event and teaches everyone the throwing-area rules.
For the rest of the day, no one enters the sector without her signal. Everyone is safe.

steps.title: Throwing-area safety first
steps.body:
- **Never enter** or cross a throwing sector while throwing is in progress.
- Throw only when the coach/official signals the area is **clear**.
- **Retrieve implements only on signal**, all together; **carry** them back — never throw them back.
- Stand behind the thrower, never in front or to the side close by.
- Use the correct implement weight for your age.

steps.title: Shot put basics (standing put)
steps.body:
- Hold the shot at the **base of the fingers** (not the palm), fingers slightly spread, thumb for support.
- Place it against the **neck under the jaw**, elbow up and out.
- Stand side-on at the back of the circle, weight on the back leg, knees bent.
- **Drive** the hips round and up, then **push** the shot away from the neck at about 35–40° with the arm, finishing with a flick of the fingers.
- It's a **put** (push), not a throw: the shot must not drop below the shoulder line or go behind it during the put.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- The circle is **2.135 m** in diameter, with a **stop board** at the front.
- A put is a foul if you touch the top of the stop board or the ground outside the circle, or leave the circle before the shot lands; you must **exit from the rear half**.
- The shot must land within the sector lines.
- Senior men's shot is **7.26 kg**; senior women's **4 kg**; youth shots are lighter.

steps.title: Progressions
steps.body: Beginners learn the **standing put**, then the **glide** (moving backwards across the circle) or **rotational** technique (spinning, like a discus thrower). Strength in the legs and core matters more than arm strength.

lessons.title: What yoga is, and how to practise safely

scenes.text: Emma, 30, from Melbourne, comes to Varanasi expecting yoga to be about bending as far as possible.
Her teacher, Shri Raghunath, spends the first class on breathing, sitting still and kindness to her own body.
He explains that asanas are just one of the eight limbs described by Patanjali.
By the end of the month Emma feels calmer than ever — and her hamstrings are looser too.

steps.title: Yoga is more than poses
steps.body:
The *Yoga Sutras of Patanjali* define yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind (*yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ*, Sutra 1.2). Patanjali describes **eight limbs (ashtanga)**:

1. **Yama** — ethical restraints (e.g., non-violence, truthfulness).
2. **Niyama** — personal observances (e.g., cleanliness, contentment).
3. **Asana** — steady, comfortable posture.
4. **Pranayama** — breath regulation.
5. **Pratyahara** — withdrawal of the senses.
6. **Dharana** — concentration.
7. **Dhyana** — meditation.
8. **Samadhi** — absorption.

The UN declared **21 June** as the **International Day of Yoga** (first observed in 2015).

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body:
This is general education, not medical advice. **Consult a doctor before starting if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma or eye problems, back or neck problems, recent surgery, are pregnant, or have any chronic condition.** Pregnant learners should follow a qualified prenatal yoga teacher.

- **Never force** a pose. Mild stretch is good; pain is a stop sign.
- Avoid inversions and strong breath-holding if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure or glaucoma.
- Stop if you feel dizzy, numb or breathless.

steps.title: Practical guidelines
steps.body:
- Practise on an **empty or light stomach** — wait about 2–3 hours after a heavy meal.
- Use a **non-slip mat** on a flat surface; comfortable clothes.
- **Breathe through the nose** steadily; never hold your breath in poses unless instructed.
- Move **slowly** into and out of poses.
- Use props — a folded blanket, cushion, wall or chair — they are tools, not 'cheating'.
- End with **Shavasana** (relaxation).

steps.title: The Common Yoga Protocol
steps.body: India's Ministry of Ayush publishes a **Common Yoga Protocol** — a short, standardised sequence of loosening practices, asanas, pranayama and meditation suitable for most people, used on International Day of Yoga. It's a good, free starting point.

lessons.title: Standing asanas: Tadasana, Vrikshasana, Trikonasana, Virabhadrasana

scenes.text: Arjun, 11, from Mysuru, keeps falling out of Vrikshasana (tree pose) in school yoga.
His teacher tells him to fix his gaze on one point on the wall — a drishti.
She also lets him rest his foot on his calf instead of his thigh.
Arjun holds the tree for 30 seconds. 'Balance starts in the mind,' says his teacher.

steps.title: Tadasana (mountain pose)
steps.body:
- Stand with feet together or hip-width, weight even across both feet.
- Thighs gently engaged, tailbone lengthening down, belly soft.
- Shoulders relaxed down, arms by your sides (or raised overhead in the common variation).
- Crown of the head lifting; breathe steadily.

It teaches **posture and awareness** — the base of all standing poses.

steps.title: Vrikshasana (tree pose)
steps.body:
- From Tadasana, shift weight to the left foot.
- Place the right sole on the inner **left calf or inner thigh — never on the knee joint**.
- Hands in prayer at the chest or raised overhead.
- Fix your **gaze** on a still point. Hold 20–30 seconds; switch sides.

**Modify**: toes on the floor with heel on the ankle, or use a wall for support.

steps.title: Trikonasana (triangle pose)
steps.body:
- Step feet wide (about a leg's length). Turn the right foot out 90°, left foot slightly in.
- Arms out at shoulder height. Reach right, then hinge at the **hip** (not the waist) and lower the right hand to the shin, ankle or a block; left arm up.
- Keep both sides of the waist long; chest open. Look up, forward or down — whatever is comfortable for your neck.

**Caution**: with neck problems, look down; with low blood pressure, come up slowly.

steps.title: Virabhadrasana II (warrior II)
steps.body:
- Feet wide; right foot out 90°, left foot slightly in.
- Bend the right knee to about 90°, **knee over the ankle**, tracking towards the second/third toe.
- Arms out at shoulder height; gaze over the front hand.
- Torso upright, shoulders relaxed. Hold 20–30 s; switch sides.

**Common mistake**: the knee collapsing inward or going far past the ankle.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Practise the four poses in sequence, holding each for 5 slow breaths per side. Notice which side is harder — that's normal, and practice evens it out.

lessons.title: Seated and lying asanas: Bhujangasana, Balasana, Setu Bandhasana, Paschimottanasana, Shavasana

scenes.text: Neha, 27, a call-centre worker in Noida, has a stiff back after night shifts.
Her doctor rules out anything serious and suggests gentle movement, including yoga.
She learns a gentle cobra, child's pose and bridge — and to skip deep forward bends for now.
Ten minutes after each shift, her back feels looser and she sleeps better.

steps.title: Bhujangasana (cobra)
steps.body:
- Lie on your stomach, legs together, tops of the feet on the floor.
- Hands under the shoulders, elbows close to the body.
- Inhale and lift the head and chest **using your back muscles**, keeping the lower ribs near the floor at first; elbows stay bent.
- Shoulders away from the ears; gaze forward.
- Hold for a few breaths, exhale down.

**Caution**: avoid or keep very low with back injury, during pregnancy, or after abdominal surgery.

steps.title: Balasana (child's pose)
steps.body:
- Kneel, big toes together, knees together or apart.
- Sit back towards the heels and fold forward, forehead on the floor or a cushion.
- Arms forward or alongside the body. Breathe into the back.

A **resting pose**. Place a cushion between thighs and calves if knees are uncomfortable.

steps.title: Setu Bandhasana (bridge)
steps.body:
- Lie on your back, knees bent, feet hip-width flat on the floor near the hips.
- Arms by your sides, palms down.
- Press into the feet and lift the hips; keep knees in line with the feet.
- Keep the **neck still** — don't turn your head while lifted.
- Hold 5 breaths; roll down slowly.

steps.title: Paschimottanasana (seated forward bend)
steps.body:
- Sit with legs straight forward (sit on a folded blanket if your back rounds).
- Inhale, lengthen the spine; exhale and **hinge from the hips**, reaching for shins, ankles or a strap around the feet.
- Keep the back as long as you can; bend the knees if needed.

**Caution**: people with disc problems or acute back pain should avoid deep forward bends unless cleared by a doctor or physio. Those with osteoporosis should avoid loaded spinal flexion.

steps.title: Shavasana (corpse pose / relaxation)
steps.body:
- Lie on your back, legs slightly apart, arms a little away from the body, palms up.
- Close your eyes; let the breath become natural.
- Scan from toes to head, relaxing each part.
- Stay 5–10 minutes. Roll to the right side and sit up slowly.

A cushion under the knees helps the lower back.

cards.back: Cobra: lift chest with back muscles, elbows bent; caution with back injury, pregnancy.
Child's pose: a resting fold; cushion for the knees if needed.
Bridge: lift hips, knees in line with feet, don't turn the neck.
Seated forward bend: hinge from hips; avoid deep bends with disc problems.
Relaxation lying on the back, 5–10 minutes; come out via the right side.

quiz.why: Gentle back-muscle lift protects the lower back.

quiz.why: Weight is on the shoulders and neck.

options: Roll to the side and sit up slowly
quiz.why: Slow transitions avoid dizziness.

lessons.title: Surya Namaskar (sun salutation)

scenes.text: Mr. and Mrs. Joshi, both 48, in Pune, decide to do Surya Namaskar on their terrace every morning.
On day one they rush 12 rounds and feel dizzy.
A yoga teacher at their society shows them to go slow, breathe with each movement and start with 3 rounds.
Six months later, they do 10 calm rounds daily — and their evening walks feel easier.

steps.title: The 12 positions (one common sequence)
steps.body:
Several versions exist; this is a widely taught one. Breathe with each movement.

1. **Pranamasana** (prayer) — exhale.
2. **Hasta Uttanasana** (raised arms) — inhale.
3. **Padahastasana** (standing forward bend) — exhale.
4. **Ashwa Sanchalanasana** (lunge, right leg back) — inhale.
5. **Parvatasana** (mountain/inverted V; some versions use plank, Dandasana) — exhale.
6. **Ashtanga Namaskara** (knees, chest, chin to floor) — hold out or natural breath.
7. **Bhujangasana** (cobra) — inhale.
8. **Parvatasana** — exhale.
9. **Ashwa Sanchalanasana** (right leg forward) — inhale.
10. **Padahastasana** — exhale.
11. **Hasta Uttanasana** — inhale.
12. **Pranamasana** — exhale.

Repeat leading with the other leg to complete one full round.

steps.title: How to practise
steps.body:
- Start with **2–3 slow rounds**, adding gradually.
- **Bend the knees** in the forward bend if your hamstrings are tight.
- Lower the back knee to the floor in the lunge.
- In Ashtanga Namaskara, lower carefully; skip it and lie flat if needed.
- Move with the breath; never hold it strenuously.
- Rest in Shavasana afterwards.

steps.title: Who should modify or avoid
steps.body: Consult a doctor first if you have **high blood pressure, heart disease, back or disc problems, hernia, wrist or shoulder injuries**, are **pregnant**, or have had recent surgery. People with high blood pressure should move slowly and avoid head-down positions held for long. Fast, many-round 'challenges' are not suitable for beginners.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do one slow round speaking the name of each position aloud. Then do it again in silence, focusing only on breathing with each movement.

lessons.title: Breathing basics: the diaphragm and slow breathing

scenes.text: Sanya, 15, in Delhi, freezes before her Class 10 mock exams — her heart races.
Her school counsellor teaches her belly breathing: hand on the belly, slow breath out longer than in.
She uses it for one minute before each paper.
'My hands still shake a bit,' she says, 'but my mind clears.'

steps.title: How breathing works
steps.body:
The **diaphragm** is a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. When it contracts, it moves down, the belly gently moves out and air flows in. When it relaxes, air flows out.

Under stress many people breathe **fast and high in the chest**. Slow, low breathing — especially with a **longer out-breath** — tends to activate the body's calming (parasympathetic) response and lower heart rate.

steps.title: Diaphragmatic (belly) breathing
steps.body:
1. Sit tall or lie on your back, knees bent.
2. One hand on the chest, one on the belly.
3. Breathe in through the nose for about **4 counts** — the **belly hand rises**, the chest hand stays mostly still.
4. Breathe out gently through the nose or pursed lips for about **6 counts**.
5. Repeat for 1–5 minutes.

Never strain; if you feel light-headed, return to normal breathing.

steps.title: Where to use it
steps.body:
- Before an exam, a performance, a penalty kick, a serve.
- When you can't sleep.
- During a disagreement, before you reply.
- After intense exercise, to recover.

If anxiety is frequent and affects daily life, talk to a counsellor or doctor; **Tele-MANAS (14416)** offers free support in India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forcing big, deep breaths (can cause dizziness).
- Lifting the shoulders to breathe.
- Expecting instant results — practise daily when calm so it works when stressed.

lessons.title: Nadi Shodhana and Bhramari

scenes.text: Rohit, 17, a goalkeeper in Pune, gets so anxious before penalty shoot-outs that he can't think.
His coach, who also teaches yoga, shows him Bhramari — the humming-bee breath.
Rohit practises in the dressing room, hums quietly for five rounds.
In the next shoot-out, he feels calm and saves two penalties.

steps.title: Nadi Shodhana / Anulom Vilom (alternate-nostril breathing)
steps.body:
1. Sit comfortably, spine tall.
2. Right hand: fold the index and middle fingers in (Vishnu mudra) or rest them on the forehead; use the **thumb** to close the right nostril and the **ring finger** to close the left.
3. Close the right nostril; **inhale through the left**.
4. Close the left; open the right; **exhale through the right**.
5. **Inhale through the right**; close it; **exhale through the left**. That's one round.
6. Do 5–10 rounds, slowly and without strain. Beginners don't hold the breath.

Skip it if your nose is blocked.

steps.title: Bhramari (humming-bee breath)
steps.body:
1. Sit comfortably, eyes closed.
2. Optionally, gently close the ears with the thumbs or index fingers (on the cartilage flap, not inside the ear).
3. Inhale through the nose.
4. Exhale slowly making a steady **'mmmm' humming sound**, like a bee, mouth closed.
5. Feel the vibration in the head; repeat 5–7 times.

Many find it calming before sleep or performance.

steps.title: Cautions
steps.body:
- Avoid Bhramari lying down, and avoid pressing into the ears if you have an ear infection.
- Stop any practice if you feel dizzy or anxious.
- People with heart or lung conditions should keep the breath easy and natural and consult their doctor before breath-retention techniques.

lessons.title: Kapalabhati and forceful techniques: who must avoid them

scenes.text: Mrs. Rao, 60, from Visakhapatnam, sees a TV programme promoting 15 minutes of Kapalabhati daily.
She has high blood pressure and a hernia operation last year.
Her daughter suggests asking her doctor first. The doctor advises gentle breathing instead.
Mrs. Rao does Nadi Shodhana and Bhramari daily and feels great — safely.

steps.title: What Kapalabhati is
steps.body: Kapalabhati ('skull-shining breath') is a **forceful, rapid exhalation** produced by sharply pulling the belly in, followed by a **passive** inhalation. It's an energising, cleansing practice traditionally described as a kriya (cleansing technique).

steps.title: How it's done (only if healthy)
steps.body:
1. Sit tall, hands on knees.
2. Take a normal breath in.
3. Exhale sharply through the nose by pulling the belly in; let the inhale happen by itself.
4. Start with **one round of 10–20 strokes**, slowly (about 1 per second), then breathe normally.
5. Increase gradually over weeks. Stop if light-headed.

Best learned from a qualified teacher.

steps.title: Who should avoid Kapalabhati
steps.body:
Avoid (or only with a doctor's permission) if you have:

- **High blood pressure or heart disease**
- **Pregnancy**, or during menstruation if it causes discomfort
- **Hernia** or recent abdominal or chest surgery
- **Epilepsy**
- **Glaucoma** or recent eye surgery
- **Acute asthma** or other lung problems, a nosebleed tendency, or a cold/blocked nose

Rapid breathing can also make some people dizzy or anxious. Children should do only gentle breathing techniques.

steps.title: Be careful with big health claims
steps.body: Pranayama can help relaxation and breathing awareness, and research suggests slow breathing practices may help stress and blood pressure in some people. But **no breathing technique cures diabetes, cancer, heart disease or other serious illnesses**. Never stop prescribed medicine because of a breathing practice.

lessons.title: Relaxation for sleep, exams and competition

scenes.text: Lakshmi, 19, a badminton player in Hyderabad, can't sleep the night before a state final.
She keeps checking her phone, which makes it worse.
She puts the phone away, does a body-scan relaxation and box breathing.
She sleeps, plays well, and decides to make the routine a habit.

steps.title: Box breathing
steps.body: In 4 – hold 4 – out 4 – hold 4. Used by many athletes and people in high-pressure jobs to steady themselves. Do 4–6 rounds. If holds feel uncomfortable, shorten them or skip them.

steps.title: Progressive muscle relaxation and body scan
steps.body:
- **Progressive muscle relaxation**: tense a muscle group gently for 5 seconds (e.g., fists), then release for 10–15 seconds, noticing the difference. Move from feet to face.
- **Body scan / Yoga Nidra-style**: lie in Shavasana and move your attention slowly through each body part, simply noticing and softening.

steps.title: Sleep habits for active people
steps.body:
- Teenagers generally need **8–10 hours**, adults **7–9 hours**.
- Same sleep and wake time daily.
- Screens off 30–60 minutes before bed; keep the room dark and cool.
- Avoid caffeine (tea, coffee, energy drinks, cola) late in the day.
- A light snack is fine; avoid heavy meals right before bed.

steps.title: A pre-competition routine
steps.body:
1. Arrive early; familiar warm-up.
2. 1–2 minutes of slow breathing (longer out-breath).
3. A cue word ('Ready', 'Smooth').
4. Picture your first action going well.
5. Accept nerves as normal — 'this is energy'.

lessons.title: Macronutrients and the balanced Indian plate

scenes.text: Ravi, 17, a kabaddi player from Rohtak, cuts out roti and rice because a gym video said 'carbs are bad'.
Within two weeks he's exhausted in training and irritable.
His coach sends him to the team dietitian, who explains that carbohydrates are an athlete's main fuel.
With rice, roti, dal, curd, vegetables and fruit back on his plate, his energy returns.

steps.title: The three macronutrients
steps.body:
- **Carbohydrates** — **4 kcal per gram**. The main fuel for high-intensity exercise and the brain. Sources: rice, roti, millets (ragi, jowar, bajra), oats, poha, potatoes, fruit, milk.
- **Protein** — **4 kcal per gram**. Builds and repairs muscles, enzymes and immune cells. Sources: dal, rajma, chana, soy, paneer, curd, milk, eggs, fish, chicken, nuts and seeds.
- **Fat** — **9 kcal per gram**. Energy for longer, lower-intensity activity, hormones, absorbing vitamins A, D, E, K. Sources: oils, ghee, nuts, seeds, fish.

**Micronutrients** (vitamins and minerals), **fibre** and **water** are essential too.

steps.title: Building a balanced plate
steps.body:
The ICMR–NIN *Dietary Guidelines for Indians* (2024) promote a varied plate built from **vegetables and fruits, whole grains or millets, pulses/eggs/fish/meat, milk or curd, and nuts and seeds**, and recommend **limiting salt, sugar and ultra-processed foods**.

A simple visual for each main meal:
- **Half** the plate: vegetables and fruit (including greens).
- **Quarter**: grains — rice, roti, millets.
- **Quarter**: protein — dal, paneer, eggs, fish, chicken, soy.
- Plus curd or milk, and a little healthy fat.

steps.title: Salt and sugar
steps.body: WHO recommends **less than 5 g of salt a day** (about a teaspoon) for adults, and keeping **free sugars below 10%** of daily energy, ideally below 5%. Pickles, papad, namkeen, instant noodles and packaged snacks are often high in salt; soft drinks and sweets are high in sugar.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cutting out a whole food group because of social-media advice.
- Skipping breakfast before morning training.
- Relying on packaged 'health' bars and drinks.
- Under-eating — athletes who don't eat enough for their training can develop **RED-S** (relative energy deficiency in sport): fatigue, frequent injuries, missed periods in girls and women, weaker bones. Talk to a doctor if you notice these signs.

lessons.title: Protein and carbohydrate needs (with vegetarian plans)

scenes.text: Gurpreet, 19, a wrestler from Punjab, is vegetarian. Friends say he 'can't get enough protein'.
His dietitian calculates his needs from his body weight and training.
His plan: milk, curd, paneer, dal, chana, soy chunks, peanuts — spread over the day.
He meets his target without any supplement and gains strength steadily.

steps.title: How much protein?
steps.body:
- **General adults**: ICMR–NIN (2020) sets the recommended dietary allowance at about **0.83 g per kg body weight per day**.
- **Active people and athletes**: sports nutrition position statements (e.g., ACSM and partners, 2016) suggest about **1.2–2.0 g/kg/day**, depending on training.
- **Spread it out**: roughly 0.25–0.3 g/kg per meal over 3–5 meals, including after training.

Most people meet their needs from food alone.

steps.title: Worked example: a 60 kg athlete
steps.body:
At 1.4 g/kg: 60 × 1.4 = **84 g protein/day**.

A vegetarian day (approximate values):
- 2 glasses milk (500 ml) ≈ 16 g
- 1 bowl curd (200 g) ≈ 7 g
- 100 g paneer ≈ 18 g
- 2 bowls dal (cooked) ≈ 14 g
- 1 bowl chana or rajma (cooked) ≈ 9 g
- 30 g soy chunks (dry weight) ≈ 15 g
- Handful of peanuts (30 g) ≈ 7 g
- Grains (roti, rice) through the day ≈ 10 g

Total ≈ **96 g** — target met. Values vary by brand and recipe; read labels.

steps.title: How much carbohydrate?
steps.body:
Carbohydrate needs rise with training:
- **Light training** (low intensity or skill-based): about **3–5 g/kg/day**.
- **Moderate** (about 1 hour a day): about **5–7 g/kg/day**.
- **High volume** (1–3 hours a day of moderate-to-high intensity): about **6–10 g/kg/day**.

These are from sports nutrition guidelines; individual needs vary.

steps.title: Plant protein tips
steps.body:
- **Combine** cereals and pulses (rice + dal, roti + rajma) — they complement each other's amino acids.
- Include **soy, milk products, peanuts** — rich, affordable sources.
- Vegans: tofu, soy, legumes, nuts, seeds; consider vitamin B12 (ask a doctor).

lessons.title: Hydration, ORS and electrolytes

scenes.text: Sneha, 32, runs her first half-marathon in humid Mumbai.
Her friend Ankit drinks litre after litre of plain water at every station, worried about dehydration.
Near the end Ankit feels confused, nauseous and bloated — medics suspect low blood sodium from over-drinking.
He recovers in the medical tent. Sneha, who drank to thirst and took some electrolytes, finishes strong.

steps.title: Why hydration matters
steps.body: Water regulates body temperature, carries nutrients and keeps blood flowing to muscles. Losing more than about **2% of body weight** as sweat can impair performance, especially in heat. Sweat also contains **sodium** (salt), which must be replaced in long, sweaty sessions.

steps.title: A practical plan
steps.body:
- **Before**: drink regularly through the day; pale-yellow urine is a rough guide.
- **During** (sessions over ~60 minutes or in heat): drink to a plan or to thirst — small, regular sips. Include sodium/electrolytes in long sessions.
- **After**: replace losses — weigh yourself before and after; for each **1 kg lost**, gradually drink about **1.25–1.5 litres** of fluid along with salty food or electrolytes.
- Buttermilk (chaas) with a pinch of salt, nimbu pani with a little salt and sugar, coconut water and ORS are useful Indian options.

steps.title: ORS: the life-saving mix
steps.body:
**Oral rehydration solution (ORS)**, recommended by WHO, contains a precise balance of salts and glucose that helps the gut absorb water. Packaged WHO-formula ORS sachets are cheap and widely available in India — mix exactly as the packet says with clean water.

ORS is also the key treatment for dehydration from diarrhoea. 'Electrolyte drinks' sold as juices often have much more sugar and are not the same as ORS — check the label.

steps.title: Too little, too much
steps.body:
- **Dehydration** signs: thirst, dark urine, headache, dizziness, tiredness, cramps.
- **Over-drinking** plain water during long events can dilute blood sodium (**hyponatraemia**) — headache, nausea, bloating, confusion, even seizures. It's a medical emergency (**112**). Don't drink far beyond thirst; don't gain weight during an event.
- Heat stroke (confusion, collapse with high body temperature) → call **112** and cool rapidly.

scenes.text: Aditi, 14, from Bengaluru, swims at 6 a.m. on an empty stomach and feels dizzy by 7.
Her coach suggests a banana and a glass of milk 30–60 minutes before.
After practice, she has idli-sambar or a paneer sandwich within an hour or two.
Her training quality improves and she stops feeling faint.

steps.title: Before training
steps.body:
- **3–4 hours before**: a normal balanced meal — e.g., rice, dal, vegetables, curd.
- **1–2 hours before**: a lighter, carb-rich snack — poha, upma, idli, a sandwich, fruit with curd.
- **30–60 minutes before**: something small and easy to digest — a banana, dates, a glass of milk, a few biscuits.
- Avoid very fatty, spicy or high-fibre foods right before if they upset your stomach. **Test new foods in training, never on match day.**

steps.title: During training
steps.body:
- Under ~60 minutes: water is usually enough.
- **Longer than 60–90 minutes**: about **30–60 g of carbohydrate per hour** (e.g., a banana ≈ 25 g, a few dates, a sports drink) plus fluid and sodium. For very long events (over 2.5 hours) some athletes trained to it use up to about 90 g/hour.

steps.title: After training
steps.body:
Within a couple of hours, have a meal or snack with **carbohydrate + protein**:
- Milk or lassi with a banana.
- Curd rice with dal.
- Egg or paneer roll.
- Chana chaat.
- Idli-sambar.

About **20–40 g of protein** after training supports muscle repair; carbohydrate refuels.

steps.title: Match day tips
steps.body:
- Eat familiar foods.
- Pack snacks and water — don't rely on venue food.
- Avoid trying a new supplement or energy drink on match day.
- Energy drinks with lots of caffeine are **not recommended for children and teens**.
