lessons.title: Myths, supplements and doping risks

scenes.text: Kabir, 20, a sprinter from Lucknow, buys an online 'herbal muscle booster' promising fast gains.
At a national event, his dope test comes back positive for a banned steroid that was hidden in the product.
Under strict liability, he is responsible for what's in his body — he's banned.
He now speaks to young athletes: 'Food first. Ask before you take anything.'

steps.title: Myths, busted
steps.body:
- **'Spot reduction'** (crunches burn belly fat): **false** — fat loss happens across the body with an energy deficit.
- **'Sweating a lot = losing fat'**: **false** — it's water.
- **'Carbs make you fat'**: excess total energy causes fat gain, not carbohydrate itself. Active people need carbs.
- **'You need protein shakes to build muscle'**: **false** — food can provide enough; shakes are just convenient.
- **'Eating after 8 pm makes you fat'**: total daily intake matters more than the clock (though late heavy meals can disturb sleep).
- **'Detox teas cleanse the body'**: the liver and kidneys do that; many detox products are just laxatives or diuretics.
- **'More protein is always better'**: beyond needs, extra protein is simply used for energy.

steps.title: Iron and anaemia
steps.body:
Anaemia is very common in India — **more than half of adolescent girls** were anaemic in NFHS-5 (2019–21). Athletes, especially girls and women, are at risk because of growth, menstruation and sweat losses.

- Iron sources: green leafy vegetables, legumes, jaggery-containing foods (small amounts), ragi, eggs, meat, fish.
- **Vitamin C** (amla, lemon, guava, oranges) with meals boosts iron absorption.
- **Tea or coffee with meals** reduces absorption — have them between meals.
- Persistent tiredness or breathlessness → get a blood test; don't self-prescribe iron tablets.

steps.title: Supplements and doping
steps.body:
- Supplements are **not tightly regulated** in many countries; studies have found some products **contaminated** with banned substances not on the label.
- Under the **strict liability** principle of the World Anti-Doping Code, **athletes are responsible for any prohibited substance found in their body**, whatever the source.
- India's **National Anti Doping Agency (NADA)** runs testing and education. Check the current **WADA Prohibited List** and ask your team doctor before taking any medicine or supplement.
- **Never** take steroids or 'injections for strength' — serious health harm and bans.
- Teens: food first; supplements only on medical advice (e.g., diagnosed deficiency).

steps.title: How to judge a nutrition claim
steps.body:
- Who's selling it? Do they profit from it?
- Does it promise fast, dramatic results? Red flag.
- Is there good research (not just testimonials)?
- What do a registered dietitian or doctor say?

When in doubt: **food first, sleep well, train smart**.

lessons.title: The pitch, the match and restarts

scenes.text: Lalremruati, 10, from Aizawl in Mizoram — where football is everywhere — joins a girls' league team.
In her first match the ball goes out over the goal line and she runs to take a throw-in. Everyone laughs kindly.
Her coach, Mr. Lalrinsanga, draws the pitch on a whiteboard and explains every line and restart.
Next week she takes a perfect corner that leads to a goal.

steps.title: The pitch
steps.body:
- A rectangle with two long **touchlines** and two short **goal lines**.
- The **halfway line** divides it; the **centre circle** has a radius of 9.15 m (10 yards).
- Each end has a **goal**: 7.32 m wide and 2.44 m high (8 yards by 8 feet).
- The **goal area** (the small box) and the **penalty area** (the big box, 16.5 m / 18 yards out) are marked in front of each goal.
- The **penalty mark** is 11 m from the goal line.
- **Corner arcs** sit at each corner.

steps.title: How a match works
steps.body:
- Two teams of **11 players**, including one **goalkeeper** each. A match can't start or continue if a team has fewer than **7**.
- Two halves of **45 minutes**, with a half-time interval (up to 15 minutes). The referee adds time for stoppages.
- A **goal** is scored when the **whole ball crosses the goal line** between the posts and under the crossbar.
- The ball is **out of play** only when the **whole ball** has crossed a touchline or goal line (on the ground or in the air) or the referee stops play.
- Many competitions allow up to **five substitutes**.

steps.title: Restarts
steps.body:
- **Kick-off**: starts each half and restarts after a goal; the ball can be kicked in any direction.
- **Throw-in**: when the ball crosses the **touchline**. Taken with **both hands, from behind and over the head**, with **both feet on the ground** on or behind the line. A goal cannot be scored directly from a throw-in.
- **Goal kick**: when the attacking team last touched the ball over the **goal line** (not a goal).
- **Corner kick**: when the defending team last touched it over their own goal line.
- **Free kicks and penalty kicks** after fouls (lesson 3).
- **Dropped ball**: after the referee stops play for, say, an injury.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the ball is out when it's on the line — it's still **in** until the whole ball crosses.
- Lifting a foot during a throw-in → a foul throw, and the other team gets the throw.
- Confusing goal kicks and corners: who touched it last decides.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Watch 10 minutes of any match and call every restart out loud before the referee signals: 'Throw-in, blue!', 'Corner, red!'. Count how many you get right.

activity.prompt: Which restart is it?

options: When part of the ball crosses the line

quiz.why: Not directly from a throw-in.

lessons.title: Offside, made simple

scenes.text: Carlos, 12, plays in São Paulo, Brazil. He keeps scoring — and the assistant referee keeps raising the flag.
'I'm not offside! I was behind the ball!' he argues. 'You were beyond the last defender when the pass was played,' says the referee.
His coach, Ana, sets up cones and has him time his runs to the moment the pass is struck.
Carlos learns to stay level and run late. His goals double — and the flags stop.

steps.title: Offside position
steps.body:
A player is in an **offside position** if:

- any part of their **head, body or feet** is in the **opponents' half** (not counting the halfway line), **and**
- that part is **nearer to the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent** (the goalkeeper usually counts as one of the last two).

Arms and hands are **not** counted (for goalkeepers too). **Level** with the second-last opponent, or level with the ball, is **onside**.

steps.title: Being in an offside position isn't an offence by itself
steps.body:
It only becomes an **offside offence** if, **at the moment a team-mate plays or touches the ball**, the player in an offside position becomes **involved in active play** by:

- **Interfering with play**: playing or touching the ball.
- **Interfering with an opponent**: e.g., blocking the keeper's line of sight or challenging for the ball.
- **Gaining an advantage**: playing a ball that rebounds off the post, the bar or an opponent, or a save.

The moment that matters is **when the pass is played**, not where the player is when they receive it.

steps.title: No offside from these
steps.body:
There is **no offside offence** if a player receives the ball directly from a **goal kick, throw-in or corner kick**. And you can **never** be offside in your **own half**.

The punishment for an offside offence is an **indirect free kick** to the defending team, from where the offence happened.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
1. Striker is 1 m beyond the last defender (keeper behind them) when the winger crosses. She scores. → **Offside.**
2. Striker is level with the last defender when the pass is played, then runs past and scores. → **Onside.**
3. Striker is in an offside position but walks back and doesn't touch the ball or affect anyone; team-mate scores. → **Not an offence.**
4. Throw-in directly to a player behind the defence. → **No offside** from a throw-in.

steps.title: How attackers beat the offside trap
steps.body:
- **Curve your run** along the defensive line, then burst as the passer's foot goes back.
- **Watch the passer and the defenders** at the same time (scan).
- Start your run from **level or behind**, not from beyond the line.

statements.s: A player in their own half can be offside.
statements.why: You can never be offside in your own half.

statements.s: Being level with the second-last defender is onside.
statements.why: Level is onside.

statements.s: You can be offside directly from a corner kick.
statements.why: No offside from corners, throw-ins or goal kicks.

statements.s: Offside position is judged when the pass is played, not when it's received.
statements.why: The moment the team-mate plays or touches the ball is what counts.

statements.s: An offside offence is punished with a penalty kick.
statements.why: It's an indirect free kick.

statements.s: A player's arms count when judging offside position.
statements.why: Arms and hands are not considered.

quiz.q: Offside position is judged at the moment…
options: A team-mate plays or touches the ball
quiz.why: It's the moment the team-mate plays the ball.

quiz.q: Which body part is NOT considered for offside position?
quiz.why: Arms and hands are ignored.

quiz.q: Restart after an offside offence?
quiz.why: An indirect free kick.

quiz.q: A player in an offside position doesn't touch the ball or affect any opponent. Offence?
quiz.why: Only involvement in active play makes it an offence.

quiz.q: From which restart can you NOT be offside?
options: A rebound off a defender's deliberate save
quiz.why: No offside from throw-ins (and goal kicks and corners).

sources: IFAB Laws of the Game, Law 11

lessons.title: Fouls, cards, free kicks and penalties

scenes.text: Imran, 15, from Kozhikode, Kerala, is frustrated after a missed chance and lunges in with studs up.
The referee shows a red card. His team plays 40 minutes with ten men and loses.
His coach explains the difference between careless, reckless and excessive force — and why tackling is a skill, not anger.
Imran apologises to the opponent. Next season he's the team's cleanest, smartest defender.

steps.title: Direct free kick offences
steps.body:
A **direct free kick** (you can score directly) is given if a player, in a way the referee considers **careless, reckless or using excessive force**: kicks, trips, pushes, jumps at, charges, strikes or tackles/challenges an opponent. Also: **holding** an opponent, **deliberate handball**, **biting or spitting** at someone, or throwing an object at the ball or a person.

- **Careless**: lack of attention → free kick only.
- **Reckless**: disregard for danger → **yellow card**.
- **Excessive force**: endangering safety → **red card**.

steps.title: Indirect free kick offences
steps.body:
An **indirect free kick** (the ball must touch another player before a goal can count — the referee raises an arm) is given for things like:

- **Playing in a dangerous manner** (e.g., a high kick near someone's head) without contact.
- **Impeding** an opponent without contact.
- **Offside**.
- The **goalkeeper** handling the ball from a **deliberate kick-pass by a team-mate** (the back-pass rule) or directly from a team-mate's throw-in.
- Preventing the keeper releasing the ball.

steps.title: Penalty kicks
steps.body: If a defending player commits a **direct free kick offence inside their own penalty area**, the attacking team gets a **penalty kick** from the penalty mark (11 m). Only the kicker and the defending goalkeeper are allowed inside the area and in front of the ball until it's kicked; the keeper must stay on the goal line between the posts, with at least part of one foot on or in line with the line at the kick.

steps.title: Yellow and red cards
steps.body:
**Yellow card (caution)** examples: reckless fouls, unsporting behaviour, dissent, delaying the restart, persistent fouling, not respecting the 9.15 m distance.

**Red card (sending off)** examples: serious foul play, violent conduct, biting/spitting, denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity by a deliberate handball or (in many cases) by a foul, offensive or abusive language or gestures, and **a second yellow card** in the same match. A sent-off player can't be replaced.

steps.title: Free kick walls and advantage
steps.body:
- Defenders must be at least **9.15 m (10 yards)** from the ball at a free kick. When three or more defenders form a wall, attackers must stay at least 1 m away from it.
- The referee may play **advantage** — letting play continue if stopping would hurt the fouled team — and can still caution the offender later.

a.text: You're the referee. A defender slides in, misses the ball, and catches the attacker's ankle with no real force. It's outside the box. Decision?

choices.label: Direct free kick, no card (careless)
choices.feedback: Right — careless challenge, free kick only.

choices.label: Red card
choices.feedback: Too harsh — no excessive force here.

b.text: Later, a defender inside his own penalty area pulls an attacker's shirt and stops him reaching a cross. Decision?

choices.label: Penalty kick
choices.feedback: Holding is a direct free kick offence; inside the area → penalty.

choices.label: Indirect free kick
choices.feedback: Holding is a direct free kick offence.

c.text: Think again: was it careless, reckless or excessive force?

choices.label: Careless → direct free kick, no card
choices.feedback: That's it.

d.text: Holding is in the direct free kick list. Where did it happen?

choices.label: Inside the penalty area → penalty kick
choices.feedback: Correct.

end1.text: Great refereeing! You judged force correctly and applied the penalty rule.

options: A free kick and a yellow card
A free kick and a red card
quiz.why: Reckless = caution.

quiz.why: 9.15 m (10 yards).

quiz.why: Second caution = sending off.

lessons.title: Positions and roles: who does what

scenes.text: Aditi, 11, in Goa, always chases the ball everywhere — like everyone else in her team.
'We look like a swarm of bees,' laughs coach Fatima. She gives each girl a zone and a job.
Aditi becomes a central midfielder: she scans, passes and links defence to attack.
The team stops swarming, starts passing, and wins its first tournament.

steps.title: Goalkeeper
steps.body: The only player who may **handle the ball** — and only **inside their own penalty area**. Jobs: stop shots, catch crosses, organise the defence by talking, and start attacks with throws and kicks. Wears a different colour.

steps.title: Defenders
steps.body:
- **Centre-backs (CB)**: the central defensive pair (or three). Win headers, tackle, block shots, mark strikers, start build-up with calm passes.
- **Full-backs (RB/LB)**: defend the wide areas, stop wingers, and **overlap** to support attacks.
- **Wing-backs**: in systems with three centre-backs, they cover the whole flank — very fit players.

steps.title: Midfielders
steps.body:
- **Defensive midfielder (DM)**: shields the defence, breaks up attacks, keeps possession simple.
- **Central midfielder (CM)**: the engine — passes, supports both attack and defence, covers huge distances.
- **Attacking midfielder (AM / 'number 10')**: plays between the opponent's lines, creates chances.
- **Wide midfielders / wingers**: provide width, dribble, cross and cut inside to shoot.

steps.title: Forwards
steps.body:
- **Centre-forward / striker**: scores goals, holds the ball up, makes runs behind the defence, presses defenders.
- **Second striker or false 9**: drops deeper to link play and drag defenders out of position.

Modern football expects **everyone** to defend and attack to some degree.

steps.title: Try this: role-watch
steps.body: Pick one player in a televised match and watch only them for 10 minutes. Note: where they stand when their team has the ball, where they go when they lose it, how often they scan (look over their shoulder). You'll learn more than watching the ball.

lessons.title: First touch and passing

scenes.text: Ravi, 12, lives in a crowded lane in Kolkata with no football ground nearby.
Every evening he passes a ball against the wall of the old warehouse: right foot, left foot, 500 passes.
At the club trials, the coach notices his first touch never lets the ball bounce away.
'Where did you train?' 'With a wall, sir.' Ravi gets selected.

steps.title: Scan before you receive
steps.body: Before the ball arrives, **look over your shoulder** to see where team-mates, opponents and space are. Top midfielders scan many times in the seconds before receiving. Scanning tells your first touch **where to go**.

steps.title: First touch
steps.body:
- Get your body **in line** with the ball, on your toes.
- Choose the surface: **inside of the foot** (most control), **outside**, **sole**, **thigh**, **chest**.
- **Cushion** the ball by relaxing the surface and drawing it back slightly as the ball arrives.
- Better: take a **directional first touch** — move the ball into space, away from pressure, ready for your next action.
- Use your **back foot** (the foot further from where the ball comes from) to open your body to the field.

steps.title: The side-foot (inside) pass
steps.body:
- **Plant foot** beside the ball, pointing at your target, about a ball's width away.
- Turn the passing foot out so the **inside of the foot** faces the target; **lock the ankle** (toes up).
- Strike the **middle of the ball** — not under it — and follow through towards the target.
- Head steady, eyes on the ball at contact.

For **longer passes**, approach at a slight angle, strike with the **instep/laces** area, lean back slightly to lift it, or keep over the ball to drive it low.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Floppy ankle** → weak, wobbly passes.
- **Plant foot too far behind** → the ball pops up.
- **Looking only at the ball** → no idea where to pass next. Scan first!
- Always passing with the strong foot — train the **weaker foot** every day.

steps.title: Wall drill
steps.body: Stand 5 m from a wall. Pass with the right foot, control with the left, pass with the left, control with the right. Count passes in 60 seconds. Then step back to 10 m. Record your best score each week.

activity.prompt: Solo passing & first-touch programme (15 minutes)

50 wall passes, left foot

options: To know where space and team-mates are before the ball arrives
quiz.why: Information before the ball arrives guides the first touch.

quiz.q: For a side-foot pass, the ankle should be…
quiz.why: A locked ankle gives a firm, accurate pass.

quiz.q: Where should the plant foot point?
quiz.why: Plant foot direction guides the pass.

quiz.q: A directional first touch…
options: Moves the ball into space ready for the next action
quiz.why: It saves time and escapes pressure.

lessons.title: Dribbling and 1v1 moves

scenes.text: Amara, 13, plays street football in Lagos, Nigeria, where the ball is always close to her feet.
She practises one move — the step-over — 1,000 times until she can do it without looking.
In a match, she drops her shoulder, steps over, and accelerates past the full-back.
Her cross is headed in. 'One move, mastered, is worth ten you half-know,' says her coach.

steps.title: Close control
steps.body:
- Keep the ball **close** — within a stride — when opponents are near.
- Use **many small touches** with the inside, outside and sole of both feet.
- Stay **low and balanced**, knees bent, arms out slightly for balance.
- **Head up** between touches to see space and defenders.

steps.title: Change of pace and direction
steps.body:
The most effective dribble is often simple: **slow down, then explode**. Defenders hate sudden acceleration.

- **Speed dribble**: in open space, push the ball further ahead with the laces/outside of the foot and sprint.
- **Cut**: drag or chop the ball sharply with the inside or outside of the foot to change direction.

steps.title: Three moves to master
steps.body:
- **Body feint / shoulder drop**: dip one shoulder as if going that way, then go the other.
- **Step-over**: circle your foot around the front of the ball (inside to outside) without touching it, then take it away with the other foot's outside.
- **Cruyff turn**: shape to pass or cross, then drag the ball behind your standing leg with the inside of the foot and turn away.

Practise slowly, then at match speed, then against a passive defender, then a real one.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dribbling with the **head down** → running into defenders or missing a free team-mate.
- Doing tricks **too far from** the defender (they have time to react) or **too close** (they can tackle).
- Dribbling in your own defensive third when a simple pass is safer.

steps.title: Cone slalom
steps.body: Set 6 cones (or slippers) 1 m apart. Dribble through using: right foot only, left foot only, inside-outside, sole rolls. Time each run and try to beat it while keeping every cone standing.

quiz.why: Losing the ball near your own goal is dangerous.

lessons.title: Shooting and finishing

scenes.text: Meera, 14, from Bhubaneswar, blasts every shot as hard as she can. Most fly over.
Her coach hangs two old bibs in the bottom corners of the goal: 'Hit the bibs, not the net.'
She learns to side-foot finishes close in and to keep her knee over the ball for driven shots.
Her goals tripled in a season — mostly low into the corners.

steps.title: Placement before power
steps.body: Most goals at every level are scored by **accurate** shots, often low and into the corners, rather than the hardest ones. A low shot is hard for a keeper to reach quickly and can deflect or be spilled.

steps.title: The driven (laces) shot
steps.body:
- Approach at a **slight angle**.
- **Plant foot beside the ball**, pointing at the target.
- **Knee and head over the ball**, toes pointed down, ankle locked.
- Strike through the **middle of the ball** with the **laces**.
- Land on your shooting foot — follow through towards the target.

Leaning back = ball goes high. Over the ball = low and hard.

steps.title: Side-foot finish and other finishes
steps.body:
- **Side-foot finish**: inside of the foot for accuracy when close to goal — like a firm pass into the corner.
- **Volley**: watch the ball onto your foot, keep over it, short swing.
- **Chip**: when the keeper rushes out, get under the ball with a short stab.
- **Composure**: pick your spot early; look at the keeper's position, then the ball at contact.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Leaning back** → over the bar.
- **Toe-poking** with no control (useful only in emergencies).
- **Changing your mind** at the last moment.
- **Looking up at contact** → mishit. Look at the ball when you strike.

steps.title: Corner targets
steps.body: Place two targets (bags, bottles) in the bottom corners of a goal. From 12 m, take 10 shots with each foot: 3 points for a target hit, 1 for on target. Record and beat your score.

quiz.q: What usually matters more for scoring?
quiz.why: Accurate, well-placed shots score most goals.

quiz.q: Why do shots fly over the bar?
quiz.why: Leaning back lifts the ball.

quiz.q: When is a chip useful?
quiz.why: A chip lifts the ball over an advancing keeper.

quiz.q: For a close-range finish, which surface gives best accuracy?
quiz.why: The side-foot is the most accurate.

lessons.title: Heading safely, concussion and staying injury-free

scenes.text: Tom, 15, in Glasgow, Scotland, clashes heads with an opponent going for a header.
He says he's fine, but he's dizzy and asks the same question twice.
His coach, Mrs. Singh, takes him off immediately — 'If in doubt, sit them out' — and he's checked by a doctor.
He follows a gradual return-to-play plan and is back two weeks later, symptom-free.

steps.title: Heading technique (for older players)
steps.body:
When heading is appropriate for your age:

- **Eyes open**, watching the ball; **mouth closed**.
- Contact with the **forehead** (the flat, hard part at the hairline), not the top of the head.
- **Neck firm**; power comes from bending the **upper body/back** and moving through the ball.
- Arms out for balance and protection — but **no elbows** into opponents.

steps.title: Limits on heading for children
steps.body: Because of concerns about repeated head impacts, several football associations — for example in **England and Scotland** — have issued guidance that limits or removes **heading practice for children**, and reduces repetitive heading in training for older players. Coaches should follow their own association's current guidance. Light balls and low numbers of repetitions are common recommendations when heading is taught.

steps.title: Concussion: if in doubt, sit them out
steps.body:
Signs after a knock to the head or body: **headache, dizziness, confusion, memory problems, nausea or vomiting, blurred vision, unusual behaviour, loss of consciousness**.

- **Remove the player** from play immediately — never return the same day.
- **Seek medical assessment**. Call **112** for loss of consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, weakness or neck pain.
- **Return gradually** under medical advice, following a step-by-step return-to-play plan.

steps.title: Preventing other common injuries
steps.body:
- Use a structured warm-up — programmes like **FIFA 11+** (running, strength, balance and jumping exercises) have been shown to reduce injuries in amateur players.
- **Shin guards** are compulsory in matches.
- Build **hamstring strength** (e.g., Nordic curls under supervision) and **ankle balance** (single-leg standing).
- Increase training load gradually; rest when you're sore or ill.

This is general education, not medical advice — see a doctor or physiotherapist for pain that persists.

choices.feedback: Right, but sooner is safer.

c.text: Off the pitch, he still has a headache. When can he play again?

choices.label: Not today; only after medical assessment and a gradual return plan
choices.feedback: Correct.

choices.label: Second half, if the headache eases
choices.feedback: Never return the same day after suspected concussion.

end1.text: You protected your friend's brain. That's real teamwork.

end2.text: He's getting help now. Next time, remove anyone with suspected concussion straight away.

courses.title: Tactics, formations, goalkeeping and the football pathway in India
courses.summary: Read the game like a coach: formations, principles of attack and defence, pressing and set pieces, the complete basics of goalkeeping, and how football is organised in India.
outcomes: Learners can describe 4-4-2, 4-3-3 and 3-5-2 and their strengths
Learners can explain width, depth, support, penetration, compactness and pressing
Learners can perform the goalkeeper's set position, catches, basic diving and distribution
Learners can describe the general pathway in Indian football

scenes.text: Daniel, a youth coach in Bengaluru, sees his team overrun in midfield every week in a 4-4-2.
He switches to 4-3-3: three central midfielders instead of two.
Now his team keeps the ball and the wingers stretch the opposition.
'Formations are just starting positions,' he tells the players. 'Principles win games.'

steps.title: Reading the numbers
steps.body: A formation lists outfield players from **defence to attack** (the goalkeeper isn't counted). **4-4-2** = 4 defenders, 4 midfielders, 2 forwards. Sometimes a middle line is split: **4-2-3-1** = 4 defenders, 2 defensive midfielders, 3 attacking midfielders, 1 striker.

Two banks of four plus two strikers.
- **Strengths**: simple, balanced, good width, two strikers to press and combine, compact defensive blocks.
- **Weaknesses**: can be outnumbered in central midfield by three-man midfields; gaps between the lines if not disciplined.

Four defenders, three central midfielders (often one holding), two wingers and a centre-forward.
- **Strengths**: control of central midfield, width from wingers, natural high pressing triangles.
- **Weaknesses**: full-backs can be exposed if wingers don't track back; the lone striker can be isolated.

steps.title: 3-5-2 (or 5-3-2 when defending)
steps.body:
Three centre-backs, two wing-backs, three central midfielders, two strikers.
- **Strengths**: extra centre-back for cover, numbers in midfield, two strikers.
- **Weaknesses**: wing-backs must cover the whole flank; space behind them can be attacked.

When defending, wing-backs drop and it becomes a **5-3-2**.

steps.title: Formations change during the game
steps.body: Teams look different **in possession** (e.g., a 4-3-3 becoming 3-2-5 when full-backs push on) and **out of possession** (dropping into a 4-5-1). Watch a team both when it has the ball and when it doesn't.

cards.back: Two banks of four, two strikers; simple and balanced, can be outnumbered centrally.
Three central midfielders, two wingers, one striker; controls midfield and presses well.
Three centre-backs, wing-backs, two strikers; becomes 5-3-2 when defending.
Two holding midfielders behind three attacking midfielders and one striker.
Not counted — numbers list outfield players from defence to attack.

quiz.why: Formations are listed defence first.

options: Being outnumbered in central midfield by a three
quiz.why: Two central midfielders vs three.

quiz.q: In a 3-5-2, who covers the full flank?
quiz.why: Wing-backs attack and defend the flank.

quiz.q: What does 'formations are starting positions' mean?
options: Shapes change in and out of possession
quiz.why: Shape is fluid during play.

lessons.title: Principles of attack and defence, pressing and set pieces

scenes.text: An under-17 team in Shillong is 2–0 down at half-time, always passing sideways.
Coach Wanshan tells them: 'Width, depth, support — and someone must run behind!'
The full-backs push wide, the striker runs in behind, and midfielders offer angles.
They win 3–2. The principles worked better than any shouting.

steps.title: Principles of attack
steps.body:
- **Width**: players spread wide to stretch defenders.
- **Depth**: players ahead of and behind the ball so there are forward and backward options.
- **Support**: angles for the ball-carrier — triangles and diamonds.
- **Penetration**: passes, dribbles or runs that break lines and go behind the defence.
- **Mobility**: movement off the ball to drag defenders.
- **Improvisation/creativity** in the final third.

steps.title: Principles of defence
steps.body:
- **Delay**: the nearest defender (the 'first defender') slows the attacker, staying goal-side.
- **Cover**: a second defender supports at an angle behind.
- **Balance**: others cover dangerous space and runners.
- **Compactness**: stay close together between and across the lines so there's little space to play through.
- **Patience and discipline**: don't dive in.

steps.title: Pressing and transitions
steps.body:
- **Pressing** means hunting the ball as a group to win it back quickly, using **triggers** (a poor touch, a backward pass, a pass to a full-back near the touchline).
- **Transitions** are the seconds after the ball changes hands. Teams that react fastest — counter-attacking or immediately counter-pressing — gain a big advantage.
- A **high press** needs fitness and coordination; one player pressing alone just gets bypassed.

steps.title: Set pieces
steps.body:
A large share of goals come from **corners, free kicks and throw-ins**.

- Attacking: planned runs, blockers (without fouling), near-post flick-ons, a target zone for the delivery.
- Defending: **zonal** (defend areas), **man-marking**, or a mix; keep someone ready for the counter-attack.
- Practise them every week — it's 'free' improvement.

steps.title: Try this: tactical notebook
steps.body: Watch a half of any match. Every 5 minutes write: Is the team wide or narrow? Who presses first? How many players are behind the ball when they lose it? You'll start seeing the game like a coach.

options: Stretches the defence to create gaps
quiz.why: Spreading out pulls defenders apart.

options: Delay the attacker and stay goal-side
quiz.why: Delay buys time for team-mates.

A goal kick to your team
quiz.why: Triggers are cues to press together.

quiz.q: Which statement about set pieces is true?
options: A large share of goals come from them
quiz.why: Set pieces produce many goals and are coachable.

lessons.title: Goalkeeping basics

scenes.text: Sana, 13, in Srinagar, is put in goal because she's tall. She's scared of the ball.
Her coach starts with soft balls and teaches the 'W' catch and how to fall safely.
He also teaches her to shout — 'Away!', 'Keeper's!', 'Man on!'
By spring, she's organising the whole defence and saved two penalties in a shoot-out.

steps.title: The set position
steps.body:
As a shot is about to be taken:

- Feet about shoulder-width, **weight on the balls of the feet**, knees bent.
- Body slightly forward, hands out in front at about waist height, palms facing the ball.
- Head still, eyes on the ball.
- Make a small **'set'** (stop moving) just before the shooter strikes, so you can push off in any direction.

**Positioning**: stand on the imaginary line from the ball to the **centre of the goal** to cover both posts best.

steps.title: Catching
steps.body:
- **Chest-to-head height**: the **'W' (contour) catch** — thumbs and index fingers nearly touching behind the ball, fingers spread.
- **Chest height**: scoop the ball into the chest, elbows close together.
- **Low balls**: get your body behind it; for a rolling ball, go down on one knee or bend with legs together, scoop it up.
- **Always get something behind the ball** — hands, body, legs.
- Secure it: bring the ball into the chest.

steps.title: Diving and getting up
steps.body:
- Step **towards** the ball (a short power step), then push off the near-side foot.
- Land on your **side**, not your elbow or stomach.
- Hands lead, the bottom hand behind the ball, top hand on top.
- If you can't hold it, **parry** it wide of the goal, not back into the middle.
- Learn on soft ground or mats, starting from kneeling.

steps.title: Distribution and communication
steps.body:
- **Throws**: rolling (bowling) for short, overarm for longer.
- **Kicks**: goal kicks and side-volleys/half-volleys from hands; short passes to defenders to build play.
- Keepers may handle the ball **only in their own penalty area**, and cannot handle a deliberate kick-pass or a direct throw-in from a team-mate.
- Recent Law changes have also tightened **how long a keeper may hold the ball** — check the current IFAB Laws for your competition.
- **Talk**: clear, early, short calls — 'Keeper's!', 'Away!', 'Time!', 'Man on!'

steps.title: Safety and common mistakes
steps.body:
- Use **proper gloves** and, for young keepers, padded clothing on hard grounds.
- **Fingers pointing at the ball** → finger injuries. Hands open, slightly angled.
- Diving **backwards** or landing on the stomach → winded, missed saves.
- Coming off the line late and hesitantly — **commit** or stay.

lessons.title: The football pathway in India

story.title: From Manipur to the national camp

scenes.text: Tomba, 12, from Imphal, plays barefoot in local tournaments every weekend.
His school enters the Subroto Cup, a famous inter-school tournament, and a scout notices him.
He joins a recognised academy, keeps studying, and plays in age-group leagues.
At 16 he's called to an age-group national camp. 'Patience and proper registration,' his coach reminds him.

steps.title: The general structure
steps.body:
- **AIFF** (All India Football Federation) is the national governing body, affiliated to FIFA.
- **State associations** organise state leagues and pick state teams (for example for the **Santosh Trophy**, the national championship for state teams).
- **District associations** run local leagues.
- **Clubs and academies** run youth teams in age-group leagues.
- Professional and semi-professional leagues include the **Indian Super League (ISL)** and the **I-League**; women play in the **Indian Women's League (IWL)**.

Structures and competition names can change; check your state association for current details.

steps.title: School football
steps.body:
- The **Subroto Cup** is a long-running national inter-school football tournament.
- School games through the **School Games Federation of India (SGFI)** include football.
- Many famous players were spotted in school or local tournaments — play as many recognised matches as possible.

steps.title: Practical steps
steps.body:
- Join a **registered club or academy** and get properly registered through the official system.
- Keep **age documents** ready; age fraud can lead to bans.
- Look for **grassroots festivals and trials** announced by official bodies.
- Keep up your studies; football also needs coaches (AIFF/AFC coaching licences), physios, analysts, referees and administrators.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body:
- Agents demanding money for guaranteed trials abroad.
- Requests to change documents.
- Pressure to leave school or home without proper contracts and parental involvement.

Genuine opportunities come through registered clubs and official trials. Talk to parents and coaches; verify everything.

a.text: An 'agent' offers a trial in Europe for ₹3 lakh, payable this week, no written contract. What do you do?

choices.label: Pay before the offer goes
choices.feedback: Pressure and no paperwork are red flags.

choices.feedback: Very wise.

choices.label: Tell parents, keep evidence, report to cybercrime helpline 1930 or police
choices.feedback: Reporting helps protect others too.

c.text: The agent refuses to give documents. What's next?

choices.label: Walk away and keep playing in recognised leagues
choices.feedback: Right — real offers can be verified.

end1.text: You avoided a scam and stayed on the genuine path.

end2.text: A hard lesson. Genuine trials don't demand big upfront payments without paperwork.
